name: Smoking Cessation
mechanism: Eliminates exposure to oxidants/carcinogens that accelerate genomic instability, vascular damage and senescence
evidence: The benchmark high-effect-size intervention: quitting before ~40 restores life expectancy nearly to never-smokers (~10 years gained quitting at 25-34), with mortality risk halving within ~10-15 years. Evidence is overwhelming, consistent and near-causal.
effect: Quitting by mid-40s regains ~6-9 yrs life expectancy (quit at 35-44 ~9 yr, 45-54 ~6 yr; life-table estimates, no CI); continuing smokers' all-cause mortality HR ~2.8-3.0 vs never-smokers (99% CI 2.4-3.3) — Jha NEJM 2013, n=202,248
human: Overwhelming consistent cohort evidence with clear age gradient
safety: Only upside; transient withdrawal; cessation aids generally safe
caveats: Observational by necessity, but causal inference robust; benefit depends on age at quitting
hallmarks: Genomic instability; Chronic inflammation; Cellular senescence; Telomere attrition
keyStudies: Jha et al., NEJM 2013 — Quitting at 25-34/35-44/45-54 gains ~10/9/6 years [https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMsa1211128]

name: Aerobic / Endurance Exercise
mechanism: Improves mitochondrial biogenesis, endothelial function, insulin sensitivity and cardiac output
evidence: Among the strongest and most consistent evidence in all of longevity: pooled cohorts (>660,000) show meeting the ~150 min/wk guideline yields ~31% lower all-cause mortality, with most benefit from the first increments, supported by RCTs on fitness/CV surrogates.
effect: All-cause mortality HR 0.69 (95% CI 0.67-0.70) at ~150 min/wk; plateau HR 0.61 (95% CI 0.59-0.62) at 3-5x minimum, no harm at >=10x — Arem JAMA Intern Med 2015, n=661,137
human: Large consistent cohorts + RCTs on surrogates
safety: Very safe; rare acute cardiac events in high-risk unscreened individuals
caveats: Mortality evidence observational, but triangulated with RCT surrogate data
hallmarks: Mitochondrial dysfunction; Chronic inflammation; Deregulated nutrient sensing; Cellular senescence
keyStudies: Arem et al., JAMA IM 2015 (n=661,137) — Guideline activity HR 0.69; up to ~39% reduction at higher doses [https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2015.0533]

name: Cardiorespiratory Fitness / VO2max
mechanism: VO2max integrates cardiac output and mitochondrial oxidative capacity — a measure of whole-body metabolic resilience
evidence: One of the strongest single predictors of mortality: in 122,007 treadmill-tested adults, higher fitness tracked with markedly lower mortality with NO upper ceiling — elite vs low fitness ~5x lower mortality, a larger adjusted effect than smoking or diabetes. Partly trainable via aerobic base + intervals.
effect: All-cause mortality HR 0.20 (95% CI 0.16-0.24), ~80% lower, elite vs low fitness; low fitness risk exceeds smoking/diabetes — Mandsager JAMA Netw Open 2018, n=122,007
human: Very large cohort with objectively measured fitness
safety: Achieving via exercise is very safe
caveats: Observational; CRF is partly genetic, so raising it may not yield the full association-sized benefit
hallmarks: Mitochondrial dysfunction; Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Mandsager et al., JAMA Netw Open 2018 (n=122,007) — Elite vs low fitness ~5x lower mortality; no upper limit [https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2018.3605]

name: Mediterranean Diet
mechanism: High MUFA, polyphenols, fiber and omega-3s reduce inflammation/oxidative stress and improve lipids and the microbiome
evidence: PREDIMED, a primary-prevention RCT in ~7,447 high-risk adults, found a MedDiet (+olive oil or nuts) cut major cardiovascular events ~30% vs control; large cohorts consistently link adherence to lower mortality. Among the strongest hard-outcome dietary evidence in longevity.
effect: Major CV events HR 0.69 (95% CI 0.53-0.91) with EVOO and HR 0.72 (95% CI 0.54-0.95) with nuts vs control — PREDIMED (Estruch NEJM 2018, republished), n=7,447
human: Primary-prevention RCT with hard CV endpoints + extensive cohorts
safety: Very safe; nutrient-dense
dose: High EVOO + nuts + vegetables/legumes/fish; low red/processed meat
caveats: PREDIMED was retracted/republished over randomization issues (results unchanged); all-cause mortality reduction not individually significant
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication; Dysbiosis; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: Estruch et al., NEJM 2018 (PREDIMED) — ~30% lower major CV events (HR 0.69-0.72) [https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1800389]

name: Resistance / Strength Training
mechanism: Mechanical loading drives muscle protein synthesis, countering sarcopenia and improving glucose/bone/myokines
evidence: Muscle-strengthening ~2x/wk is associated with ~10-21% lower all-cause mortality (J-shaped, peak ~30-60 min/wk), and combining with aerobic exercise gives ~40% lower mortality. RCTs robustly show strength/function gains and sarcopenia treatment.
effect: All-cause mortality RR 0.85 (95% CI 0.79-0.93) for muscle-strengthening alone; RR 0.60 (95% CI 0.54-0.67) combined with aerobic — Momma BJSM 2022
human: Cohort mortality data + strong RCT evidence for strength/function
safety: Very safe with proper form; valsalva BP spikes in uncontrolled hypertension
caveats: Mortality evidence observational; muscle-mass gains modest in oldest-old; best added to aerobic
hallmarks: Stem cell exhaustion; Loss of proteostasis; Deregulated nutrient sensing; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: Momma et al., BJSM 2022 — ~30-60 min/wk: 10-20% lower mortality [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35228201/] | Saeidifard 2019 — RT+aerobic HR 0.60 all-cause mortality [https://doi.org/10.1177/2047487319850718]

name: Sleep Optimization
mechanism: Adequate sleep enables glymphatic clearance, metabolic/immune regulation and restrains inflammation
evidence: Large meta-analyses show a U-shaped sleep-mortality curve with a nadir ~7 hours; healthy-sleep scores predict multi-year life-expectancy gains. Consistent and mechanistically grounded, but observational (long sleep is heavily confounded by illness).
effect: U-shaped all-cause mortality: RR 1.06/h (95% CI 1.04-1.07) for short sleep and RR 1.13/h (95% CI 1.11-1.15) for long sleep, nadir ~7h — Yin et al. JAHA 2017 dose-response meta-analysis
human: Large consistent cohorts; RCTs only on surrogate markers
safety: No downside to healthy sleep (sedatives carry own risks)
caveats: Long-sleep risk largely reverse causation; causal benefit of extending short sleep unproven by RCT
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication; Loss of proteostasis
keyStudies: Yin et al., JAHA 2017 — U-shaped; short and long sleep raise mortality vs 7h [https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/JAHA.117.005947]

name: Empagliflozin / Dapagliflozin
mechanism: Glucosuria, natriuresis and mild ketosis reduce cardiac/renal stress beyond glucose lowering
evidence: Among the strongest HUMAN hard-outcome evidence in the field: large RCTs cut cardiovascular death, all-cause mortality and kidney-disease progression, including in non-diabetics. But trials enrolled people with established disease, not healthy aging.
effect: All-cause mortality HR 0.68 (95% CI 0.57-0.82) empagliflozin in T2D+CVD (EMPA-REG, n=7,020); HR 0.69 (95% CI 0.53-0.88) dapagliflozin in CKD (DAPA-CKD, n=4,304)
human: Multiple positive hard-outcome RCTs, some incl. non-diabetics
safety: Genital/urinary infections, volume depletion, rare euglycemic DKA; no amputation signal
caveats: Mortality benefit shown only in diseased populations; untested for lifespan extension in healthy people
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Chronic inflammation; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: EMPA-REG, NEJM 2015 — All-cause mortality HR 0.68; CV death HR 0.62 in diabetics with CVD [https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1504720] | DAPA-CKD, NEJM 2020 — All-cause mortality HR 0.69 in CKD +/- diabetes [https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2024816]

name: Omega-3 Fatty Acids (EPA/DHA)
mechanism: Anti-inflammatory eicosanoids/resolvins; membrane and lipid effects
evidence: Among the strongest longevity-relevant supplement evidence: in DO-HEALTH, 1 g/d slowed several epigenetic aging clocks and reduced infections/falls, and combined with vitamin D + exercise cut invasive cancer. CV outcomes are mixed (generic fish oil failed VITAL/ASCEND; Rx high-dose EPA cut MACE in REDUCE-IT).
effect: Epigenetic-clock slowing ~3-4 mo/3yr (GrimAge2 d -0.32, 95% CI -0.59 to -0.06) in DO-HEALTH (n=777); CV benefit only with Rx EPA — MACE HR 0.75 (95% CI 0.68-0.83), REDUCE-IT 2019
human: Multiple large RCTs; positive on aging biomarkers, mixed on CV
safety: Very safe; mild GI; modest AFib/bleeding signal at high dose
caveats: Generic fish oil failed CV hard-outcome trials; clock benefit not yet proven to extend lifespan
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: DO-HEALTH, Nature Aging 2025 — 1 g/d slowed PhenoAge/GrimAge2/DunedinPACE clocks [https://www.nature.com/articles/s43587-024-00793-y] | DO-HEALTH, JAMA 2020 (n=2,157) — Omega-3 cut infections ~11% and falls ~10%; no benefit on primary bone/memory/muscle endpoints [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33170239/] | DO-HEALTH, Frontiers in Aging 2022 — 3-way combo cut invasive cancer 61% (HR 0.39) [https://doi.org/10.3389/fragi.2022.852643]

name: Daily Steps / Walking
mechanism: Accumulated low-intensity movement improves vascular function, glucose handling and reduces sedentary time
evidence: A device-measured meta-analysis (~47,000) found mortality declines with more steps, plateauing ~6,000-8,000/day for older adults — debunking the arbitrary 10,000 target. Each +1,000 steps/day ~15% lower mortality. Observational but device-measured.
effect: All-cause mortality HR 0.47 (95% CI 0.39-0.57), ~53% lower, highest vs lowest step quartile; optimum plateaus ~6,000-8,000/day (>=60y), ~8,000-10,000/day (<60y) — Paluch Lancet Public Health 2022
human: Strong device-measured cohort data; no RCT (impractical)
safety: Extremely safe
caveats: Observational; reverse causation (frail people walk less) likely inflates low-step risk
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Deregulated nutrient sensing; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: Paluch et al., Lancet PH 2022 — Mortality plateaus ~6,000-8,000 steps/day (>=60 yr) [https://doi.org/10.1016/S2468-2667(21)00302-9]

name: Alcohol Moderation / Abstention
mechanism: Ethanol/acetaldehyde are carcinogens promoting DNA damage, hepatic injury and inflammation; reducing intake lowers this burden
evidence: The 2023 Zhao/Naimi meta-analysis (107 cohorts, ~4.8M) overturned the old 'J-curve': after correcting for abstainer-bias, low-moderate drinking showed no mortality benefit, with clear harm above ~25 g/d (women)/45 g/d (men). Mendelian randomization supports monotonic harm. Consensus: no safe level for cancer.
effect: No mortality benefit at low intake — RR 0.93 (95% CI 0.85-1.01, NS) for 1.3-24 g/d vs lifetime nondrinkers; harm >=25 g/d women (RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.08-1.36) and >=45 g/d men (RR 1.15, 95% CI 1.03-1.28) — Zhao/Naimi JAMA Netw Open 2023, n=4.8M
human: Bias-corrected meta-analysis + Mendelian randomization converge against the J-curve
safety: Alcohol is a Group 1 carcinogen; harms rise with dose; dependence risk
caveats: Prior 'protective' findings reflected abstainer bias; residual debate on CV-specific endpoints only
hallmarks: Genomic instability; Chronic inflammation; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: Zhao/Naimi, JAMA Netw Open 2023 — No mortality benefit at low/moderate intake; harm at higher [https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.6185]

name: Vitamin D3
mechanism: VDR-mediated gene regulation; calcium, immune and possible telomere/inflammation effects
evidence: Large RCTs (VITAL, ASCEND) show 2000 IU/d does not reduce total cancer, CV events or all-cause mortality in mostly-replete people. Meta-analyses show a modest ~12% reduction in cancer MORTALITY and lower autoimmune disease. Benefit concentrated in the deficient.
effect: Total cancer mortality RR 0.87 (95% CI 0.79-0.96), ~13% lower (daily dosing); no effect on cancer incidence (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.93-1.03); negligible CV/all-cause in replete people — Keum Ann Oncol 2019
human: Definitive RCTs: neutral for most hard endpoints except modest cancer-mortality signal
safety: Safe at <=4000 IU/d; high bolus dosing raises fall/fracture risk
caveats: Benefit largely limited to deficient people; routine high-dose in replete adults shows no mortality benefit
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication; Telomere attrition
keyStudies: VITAL, NEJM 2019 (n=25,871) — No reduction in cancer incidence or major CV events [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30415629/] | Keum et al. meta-analysis — Daily vitamin D cut cancer mortality ~12-13% [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30796437/]

name: High-Intensity Interval Training
mechanism: Brief near-maximal efforts maximally stress cardiac output and mitochondria, producing potent VO2max gains per unit time
evidence: The Generation 100 RCT (n=1,567, age 70-77, 5 yr) found overall mortality did not differ significantly, but the HIIT subgroup had the lowest (non-significant) mortality and best VO2max/quality-of-life gains. HIIT reliably outperforms moderate training for raising VO2max.
effect: Non-significant mortality reduction; superior VO2max gains
human: One large RCT (underpowered for mortality) + many fitness RCTs
safety: Safe in older adults under guidance; higher acute risk than moderate exercise
caveats: Flagship RCT underpowered for mortality with an active control; clearest benefit is VO2max
hallmarks: Mitochondrial dysfunction; Deregulated nutrient sensing; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Stensvold et al., BMJ 2020 (Gen100) — HIIT subgroup ~3% vs ~4.7-6% control mortality (NS); best fitness gains [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33028588/]

name: Social Connection
mechanism: Strong social ties buffer chronic stress, lower inflammatory/neuroendocrine load and promote healthy behaviors
evidence: Holt-Lunstad's meta-analyses found strong social relationships associated with ~50% greater survival odds, with isolation/loneliness raising mortality ~26-32% — effect sizes rivaling smoking. Observational; intervention trials aren't powered for mortality.
effect: Stronger social ties: OR 1.50 (95% CI 1.42-1.59) for survival, rising to OR 1.91 (95% CI 1.63-2.23) for complex social integration — Holt-Lunstad PLoS Med 2010 (148 studies, n=308,849)
human: Large meta-analytic cohort data; no mortality-powered RCT
safety: No risk
dose: Regular meaningful relationships and community engagement
caveats: Observational; reverse causation/confounding; causal mortality reduction not shown by RCT
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Holt-Lunstad et al., PLOS Med 2010 (148 studies) — Strong ties ~50% higher survival odds (OR 1.50) [https://journals.plos.org/plosmedicine/article?id=10.1371/journal.pmed.1000316] | Holt-Lunstad et al., Perspect Psychol Sci 2015 — Isolation OR 1.29, loneliness 1.26, living alone 1.32 (~26-32% higher mortality) [https://doi.org/10.1177/1745691614568352]

name: Statins
mechanism: Lower LDL cholesterol; pleiotropic anti-inflammatory/endothelial effects
evidence: Backed by very large RCTs and CTT meta-analyses with hard endpoints: ~10% lower all-cause mortality per 1 mmol/L LDL drop, mainly in secondary prevention. Benefit in low-risk primary prevention and the very elderly is smaller. Targets cardiovascular disease, not aging per se.
effect: All-cause mortality RR 0.90 (95% CI 0.87-0.93) and major vascular events RR 0.78 (95% CI 0.76-0.80) per 1 mmol/L LDL-C reduction — CTT Lancet 2010 (26 trials, n~170,000)
human: Strong for CV mortality; modest/uncertain in low-risk primary prevention
safety: Generally safe; myalgia, rare myopathy, small diabetes risk
caveats: Targets atherosclerosis not aging broadly; benefit risk-dependent; not a validated geroprotector
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: CTT, Lancet 2010 (>170k) — ~10% lower all-cause mortality per 1 mmol/L LDL reduction [https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(10)61350-5] | JUPITER, NEJM 2008 — Rosuvastatin cut all-cause mortality HR 0.80 in high-CRP adults [https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0807646]

name: Semaglutide
mechanism: Activates GLP-1 receptors to reduce appetite/weight, improve glucose control and lower inflammation
evidence: Genuine large-RCT hard outcomes: SELECT cut major cardiovascular events 20% in non-diabetic adults with obesity and prior CVD — the first proof that treating obesity pharmacologically improves CV outcomes. Untested for lifespan; concerns include muscle-mass loss and weight regain on stopping.
effect: MACE HR 0.80 (95% CI 0.72-0.90), 20% lower, in non-diabetic obesity; mean weight -9.4% vs -0.9% placebo — SELECT (Lincoff NEJM 2023), n=17,604
human: Strong CV hard-outcome RCT; no aging-endpoint trial
safety: GI effects, pancreatitis/gallbladder risk, lean-mass loss, weight regain after stopping; rodent thyroid signal
caveats: No aging-specific evidence; muscle loss; dependence on continued use
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: SELECT, NEJM 2023 (n=17,604) — MACE HR 0.80 in non-diabetic obesity; ~9% weight loss [https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2307563]

name: Rapamycin
mechanism: Inhibits mTORC1, mimicking caloric restriction and inducing autophagy
evidence: The most reproducible pharmacological lifespan extender in animals and the standout of the NIA Interventions Testing Program, working even when started late in life. Human trials (PEARL, RTB101) show safety and immune/biomarker effects but no lifespan data.
effect: +10-26% median lifespan (mice, dose-dependent)
human: Phase-2 safety/biomarker RCTs; widely used off-label; no lifespan RCT
safety: Generally safe at low intermittent doses; immunosuppression, mouth sores, glucose/lipid effects at higher doses
caveats: No human lifespan RCT; optimal dose/schedule unresolved — most-hyped longevity drug yet thin human proof
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Disabled macroautophagy; Cellular senescence; Loss of proteostasis
keyStudies: Harrison et al., Nature 2009 (ITP) — First drug to extend mouse lifespan started in old age; +9% male/+14% female at age of 90% mortality [https://doi.org/10.1038/nature08221] | Miller et al., Aging Cell 2014 (ITP) — Dose-dependent median lifespan +23% male/+26% female at 42 ppm [https://doi.org/10.1111/acel.12194] | PEARL RCT 2024 (n=114) — Low-dose weekly rapamycin safe over 48 weeks; lean-mass/pain gains in women [https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.08.21.24312372v1]

name: Caloric Restriction
mechanism: Lowers nutrient-sensing (insulin/IGF-1, mTOR), induces autophagy and stress resistance
evidence: The most-studied lifespan intervention in animals. In humans, the CALERIE-2 RCT (~12% restriction, 2 yr) slowed the DunedinPACE pace-of-aging clock, reduced cardiometabolic risk and regenerated thymic volume — but on surrogate endpoints, with low adherence to deep restriction.
effect: Large in animals; modest biological-age slowing in humans
human: Landmark RCT (surrogate) + primate studies
safety: Risk of muscle/bone loss, hunger, cold intolerance, disordered eating if overdone
caveats: Hard-outcome human benefit unproven; sustained deep restriction has low adherence
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Chronic inflammation; Disabled macroautophagy; Stem cell exhaustion; Epigenetic alterations
keyStudies: Waziry et al., Nat Aging 2023 (CALERIE-2) — Slowed DunedinPACE ~2-3% over 2 years [https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-022-00357-y] | Spadaro/Dixit, Science 2022 — Increased thymic functional volume [https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abg7292]

name: Nut Consumption
mechanism: Unsaturated fats, fiber, plant protein, magnesium and polyphenols lower LDL, improve endothelial function/insulin sensitivity and reduce inflammation
evidence: Large cohorts (Bao 2013 ~119k; Aune 2016 meta ~819k) show ~20% lower all-cause mortality with regular intake, and PREDIMED randomized high-CV-risk adults to a Mediterranean diet plus mixed nuts with a hard CV-event reduction. Limitation: mortality data are observational, and the RCT tests a whole pattern (with added nuts), not nuts in isolation.
effect: ~20-22% lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.73-0.86); RCT CV events HR 0.72 (0.54-0.97)
human: Strong cohort mortality data plus an RCT with hard cardiovascular endpoints
safety: Very safe; calorie-dense but no net weight gain at typical portions; tree-nut/peanut allergy is the one contraindication
status: Endorsed by dietary guidelines; component of the Mediterranean pattern
caveats: Mortality figures observational; the hard-endpoint RCT (PREDIMED) tests a whole pattern not nuts alone (and was retracted/re-analyzed 2018)
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Deregulated nutrient sensing; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: Bao et al., NEJM 2013 (NHS+HPFS, n=118,962) — Nuts 7+/wk vs never: total mortality HR 0.80 (95% CI 0.73-0.86) [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24256379/] | Aune et al., BMC Medicine 2016 (20 studies, n=819,448) — Per 28 g/day: all-cause mortality RR 0.78 (95% CI 0.72-0.84) [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5137221/]

name: Dietary Fiber
mechanism: Fermentable fiber feeds gut microbiota producing anti-inflammatory short-chain fatty acids (butyrate); viscous fiber slows glucose absorption, binds bile acids to lower LDL, and increases satiety
evidence: The WHO-commissioned Reynolds (Lancet 2019) synthesis pooled ~135 million person-years across 185 prospective studies plus 58 RCTs and found the highest fiber consumers had 15-30% lower all-cause and CV mortality with a near-linear dose-response judged potentially causal (GRADE moderate). Mortality outcomes are predominantly observational; the included RCTs measured intermediate cardiometabolic markers.
effect: ~15-30% lower all-cause mortality (highest vs lowest intake); large cohorts converge near RR 0.78
human: Strong, consistent observational mortality evidence; RCTs support only intermediate markers
safety: Very safe; GI tolerance the main issue if increased too fast (escalate gradually with fluids)
dose: ~25-29 g/day or more (most adults get only ~15-20 g) from whole grains, legumes, vegetables, fruit
caveats: Mortality evidence mostly observational with likely healthy-user confounding; RCT support limited to cardiometabolic surrogates
hallmarks: Dysbiosis; Chronic inflammation; Deregulated nutrient sensing
keyStudies: Reynolds et al., Lancet 2019 (WHO meta-analysis) — Highest vs lowest fiber: 15-30% lower all-cause + CV mortality; ~13 fewer deaths/1,000 [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30638909/] | Park et al. (NIH-AARP, n=388,122), Arch Intern Med 2011 — Highest vs lowest quintile all-cause mortality RR ~0.78 (95% CI 0.73-0.82) [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3513325/]

name: Creatine
mechanism: Replenishes phosphocreatine/ATP in muscle and brain, supporting energy availability
evidence: Among the best-evidenced supplements for the aging musculoskeletal system: meta-analyses show creatine PLUS resistance training increases strength and lean mass in older adults more than training alone — relevant to sarcopenia. Cognitive benefits are plausible but unsettled.
effect: Meaningful added strength/lean-mass with training; cognition uncertain
human: Robust RCT/meta-analytic evidence for muscle (with training)
safety: Very safe, extensively studied; mild water-weight gain; no kidney harm in healthy people
caveats: Muscle benefit largely requires concurrent resistance training; not a standalone longevity drug
hallmarks: Mitochondrial dysfunction; Stem cell exhaustion; Loss of proteostasis
keyStudies: Meta-analyses, creatine + RT in older adults — Greater strength/lean-mass gains vs training + placebo [https://doi.org/10.1186/s11556-025-00392-9]

name: Cardiovascular Polypill
mechanism: One daily tablet lowers LDL and blood pressure (plus antiplatelet if aspirin included), maximizing long-term adherence
evidence: Large randomized trials with hard CV endpoints converge on ~30% fewer major cardiovascular events: TIPS-3 (n=5,713, placebo-controlled primary prevention) and PolyIran (50,045, pragmatic cluster-RCT), pooled RR 0.71. Its innovation is adherence/simplicity, not a novel mechanism, and all-cause mortality was not individually significant.
effect: ~21-34% fewer major CV events (pooled RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.63-0.80); all-cause mortality not individually significant
human: Strong hard-outcome RCT evidence for CV-event reduction in primary prevention
safety: Well tolerated; modest excess dizziness/hypotension; aspirin versions carry bleeding risk
dose: One daily fixed-dose tablet (statin + 2-3 antihypertensives +/- low-dose aspirin)
status: Marketed in several countries; on the WHO Essential Medicines List
caveats: Proven on CV events not all-cause mortality; an adherence/packaging strategy over drug classes already listed separately (statins, ACEi/ARBs)
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Yusuf et al. (TIPS-3), NEJM 2021 — Primary CV composite HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.63-1.00); polypill+aspirin HR 0.69 (0.50-0.97) [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33186492/] | Roshandel et al. (PolyIran), Lancet 2019 — Major CV events HR 0.66 (95% CI 0.55-0.80); high-adherence HR 0.43 (0.33-0.55) [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31448738/]

name: Hearing Aid Use
mechanism: Restoring auditory input reduces effortful-listening cognitive load, reverses sensory deprivation, sustains social engagement and slows temporal-lobe atrophy
evidence: The ACHIEVE RCT (Lancet 2023, n=977) found a hearing intervention did NOT slow 3-year global cognitive decline overall, but in the prespecified higher-risk ARIC subgroup it slowed decline ~48%. This sits atop the Lancet Commission ranking hearing loss as the largest modifiable midlife dementia risk factor and a 31-study observational meta-analysis (HR 0.81). The primary RCT endpoint was null overall, so the benefit is a subgroup/observational signal.
effect: High-risk RCT subgroup ~48% slower 3-yr cognitive decline; pooled observational HR 0.81 (0.76-0.87)
human: Mixed RCT (null primary, strong high-risk subgroup) + consistent observational cognition data
safety: Essentially no risk; non-invasive; worst case minor discomfort/feedback/cost
dose: Daily wear of fitted hearing aids for adults with hearing loss; benefit greatest with earlier, consistent use
status: OTC hearing aids available without prescription in the US since Oct 2022
caveats: The flagship RCT's primary endpoint was null in the full cohort — the 48% benefit is a high-risk subgroup finding; most supporting data are observational
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Lin et al. (ACHIEVE), Lancet 2023 — 3-yr cognition: full cohort null; high-risk ARIC subgroup ~48% slower decline (diff 0.191, 95% CI 0.022-0.360) [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37478886/] | Yeo et al. meta-analysis (31 studies, n=137,484), JAMA Neurol 2023 — Hearing-device use: cognitive decline HR 0.81 (95% CI 0.76-0.87) [https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2799139]

name: CoQ10 / Ubiquinol
mechanism: Electron-transport-chain cofactor and lipid-phase antioxidant
evidence: Standout is KiSel-10: CoQ10 200 mg + selenium for 4 years roughly halved cardiovascular mortality in elderly Swedes, persisting at 12-year follow-up. Combined with selenium (confound) and strongest in deficient/older/cardiac populations.
effect: CV mortality HR 0.51 (95% CI 0.36-0.74), ~49% lower (5.9% vs 12.6%), with CoQ10 200mg + selenium 200ug/d in selenium-low elderly — KiSel-10 (Alehagen 2013), n=443
human: Positive hard-outcome RCTs (elderly/HF), but bundled with selenium
safety: Very safe; mild GI; interacts with warfarin
caveats: Flagship benefit came combined with selenium in a likely-deficient cohort
hallmarks: Mitochondrial dysfunction; Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Alehagen et al., KiSel-10 — CoQ10+selenium cut CV mortality ~50% (HR 0.51), persisting 12 yr [https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0193120] | Q-SYMBIO, JACC HF 2014 — CoQ10 reduced major cardiac events in heart failure [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jchf.2014.06.008]

name: Menopausal Hormone Therapy
mechanism: Replaces declining estrogen (with progestogen to protect the endometrium); ER signaling across bone, vasculature, brain
evidence: The 'timing hypothesis' (WHI re-analyses, ELITE) holds that starting MHT near menopause (<60y) is associated with lower all-cause mortality and possibly reduced coronary risk, whereas late initiation raises stroke/VTE risk. It is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and prevents fractures; the longevity signal is associational.
effect: Best therapy for hot flushes; reduces fractures; possible mortality benefit if started early
human: Large RCTs + cohorts; favorable for symptomatic women starting near menopause
safety: Small absolute increases in breast cancer (combined oral), VTE, stroke; transdermal lowers VTE risk
dose: Lowest effective dose (transdermal estradiol + progesterone if uterus)
caveats: Window-of-opportunity matters; not a blanket anti-aging therapy; real (if small) risks
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation; Stem cell exhaustion
keyStudies: Manson et al., WHI, JAMA 2017 — No increase in all-cause/CV/cancer mortality over 18 yr [https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2017.11211] | Hodis et al., ELITE, NEJM 2016 — Early estradiol slowed carotid IMT; late did not [https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1505241]

name: Finnish Sauna Bathing
mechanism: Heat stress induces heat-shock proteins, improves endothelial function, lowers BP — a mild cardiovascular load
evidence: The Finnish KIHD cohort links 4-7 sauna sessions/wk to ~40% lower all-cause and sharply lower cardiovascular/sudden-cardiac mortality. But the one controlled trial (8 weeks, CAD patients) was NULL on vascular surrogates, so causality and healthy-user bias remain unresolved.
effect: All-cause mortality HR 0.60 (95% CI 0.46-0.80) at 4-7 sessions/wk vs 1/wk; fatal CVD HR 0.50 (95% CI 0.33-0.77) — Laukkanen JAMA Intern Med 2015 (KIHD, n=2,315 men); RCT surrogate data ~null
human: Strong cohorts; only RCT negative on vascular surrogates
safety: Generally safe; dehydration, orthostatic hypotension, caution with unstable cardiac disease
caveats: Cohort benefit likely confounded by healthy-user bias; the one RCT showed no vascular benefit
hallmarks: Loss of proteostasis; Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Laukkanen et al., JAMA IM 2015 (KIHD) — 4-7/wk vs 1/wk: ~40% lower all-cause mortality [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25705824/] | Lee/Laukkanen, J Appl Physiol 2023 RCT — No change in FMD/BP/stiffness in CAD (null) [https://doi.org/10.1152/japplphysiol.00322.2023]

name: Coffee / Caffeine
mechanism: Chlorogenic acids and caffeine act as antioxidants, activate AMPK/autophagy and suppress NF-kB inflammation while improving glucose/lipid metabolism
evidence: Very large prospective cohorts (EPIC ~521k; UK Biobank ~498k) and a 40-study dose-response meta-analysis (~3.85M) consistently show ~10-18% lower all-cause mortality at ~3-4 cups/day, with decaffeinated coffee showing similar benefit (implicating non-caffeine compounds). All evidence is observational, so residual confounding and reverse causation can't be excluded; no long-term mortality RCT exists.
effect: ~12-18% lower all-cause mortality at ~3-4 cups/day (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.82-0.89); observational
human: Large, consistent observational mortality evidence across continents; not proven causal
safety: Safe for most adults up to ~400 mg caffeine/day; caveats: pregnancy (<=200 mg/day), anxiety/insomnia, unfiltered coffee raises LDL via cafestol
status: Strong, widely-accepted observational evidence; likely modest net benefit at moderate intake
caveats: Entirely observational — coffee drinkers differ systematically and the ill cut back (reverse causation), so causality is unestablished
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Deregulated nutrient sensing; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: Kim, Je & Giovannucci, Eur J Epidemiol 2019 (40-study meta, 3.85M) — All-cause mortality nadir at ~3.5 cups/day RR 0.85 (95% CI 0.82-0.89) [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31055709/] | Loftfield et al. (UK Biobank, n=498,134), JAMA Intern Med 2018 — 2-3 cups/day HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.84-0.93); decaf also inverse; independent of caffeine-metabolism genotype [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6143111/]

name: Tirzepatide
mechanism: Co-agonizes GIP and GLP-1 receptors for greater weight loss and glycaemic control
evidence: Produces the largest pharmacological weight loss yet (~22.5% in SURMOUNT-1) and broad cardiometabolic improvement; the dedicated morbidity/mortality trial (SURMOUNT-MMO) is ongoing, so hard aging-relevant outcomes are not yet read out.
effect: Up to ~22.5% weight loss; mortality data pending
human: Strong surrogate data; morbidity/mortality trial not yet reported
safety: GI effects, pancreatitis/gallbladder risk, lean-mass loss, weight regain; rodent thyroid signal
caveats: Hard-outcome/mortality data pending; no aging-endpoint trial; muscle-loss concern
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: SURMOUNT-1, NEJM 2022 — Up to 22.5% weight loss over 72 weeks [https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2206038] | SURPASS-CVOT, 2025 — Non-inferior to dulaglutide for MACE (HR ~0.92) [https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2505928]

name: ACE Inhibitors / ARBs
mechanism: Block angiotensin-II signaling, lowering BP and RAS-driven oxidative stress, fibrosis and inflammation
evidence: Unusual breadth: RAS inhibition extends lifespan from worms to rats (ramipril ~doubled hypertensive-rat lifespan), captopril was a positive ITP hit, and ACEi/ARBs cut CV mortality in high-risk humans (HOPE). No trial in healthy normotensives.
effect: Up to ~2x lifespan in hypertensive rats; human all-cause HR ~0.84 (high-risk)
human: CV mortality benefit in high-risk groups; no healthy-aging trial
safety: ACEi: cough, hyperkalaemia, angioedema; ARBs better tolerated; both contraindicated in pregnancy
caveats: Human mortality data in diseased groups; lifespan benefit in healthy people untested
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: Strong et al., ITP 2022 — Captopril +4-5% female mouse lifespan [https://doi.org/10.1111/acel.13724] | HOPE, NEJM 2000 — Ramipril cut all-cause mortality HR 0.84 in high-risk patients [https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM200001203420301]

name: Nicotinamide (NAM)
mechanism: Salvaged directly to NAD+ via NAMPT; at high doses inhibits sirtuins/PARPs
evidence: Unusual for a positive hard-outcome RCT — but for skin-cancer prevention, not aging: ONTRAC showed 500 mg twice daily cut new non-melanoma skin cancers 23% in high-risk patients. Reflects DNA-repair/energy support in skin; a later transplant trial was negative.
effect: 23% fewer non-melanoma skin cancers (hard endpoint); not an established longevity effect
human: Strong cancer-prevention RCT; not shown to extend healthspan
safety: Very safe at 500 mg x2/day (no flushing); very high doses risk hepatotoxicity/sirtuin inhibition
caveats: Proven benefit is skin-cancer prevention, not anti-aging; high doses inhibit sirtuins
hallmarks: Genomic instability; Deregulated nutrient sensing; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: Chen et al., NEJM 2015 (ONTRAC) — -23% non-melanoma skin cancer over 12 months [https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1506197]

name: Testosterone Replacement Therapy
mechanism: Restores serum testosterone via androgen-receptor signaling; affects muscle, bone, libido, erythropoiesis
evidence: The large TRAVERSE RCT found TRT non-inferior to placebo for major cardiac events in hypogonadal men, settling a CV-safety question — but with MORE atrial fibrillation, AKI, PE and (unexpectedly) fractures. It improves libido/lean mass/BMD in true deficiency, but there is NO evidence it extends lifespan and it should not be an anti-aging tonic in men with normal testosterone.
effect: Clear gains in hypogonadism; no longevity benefit; net harms in higher-risk older men
human: Definitive large RCT; CV-safe at replacement doses but not life-extending
safety: Erythrocytosis, atrial fibrillation, fracture/PE risk, infertility, sleep-apnea worsening
caveats: Benefit only in true deficiency, with real adverse effects and no survival gain
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Stem cell exhaustion
keyStudies: Lincoff et al., TRAVERSE, NEJM 2023 (n=5,246) — MACE non-inferior to placebo; more atrial fibrillation, AKI and PE [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37326322/] | TRAVERSE Fracture sub-trial, NEJM 2024 — More clinical fractures on testosterone (3.5% vs 2.5%) [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38231621/]

name: Zoledronate / Bisphosphonates
mechanism: Inhibits bone resorption; emerging senolytic/senomorphic and DNA-damage-resilience effects
evidence: Beyond fracture prevention, annual zoledronic acid cut mortality 28% after hip fracture (HORIZON-RFT) — more than fracture reduction explains, prompting geroscience interest, with preclinical senolytic activity now reported. Mortality signal is in frail post-fracture patients.
effect: All-cause mortality -28% post-fracture; senolytic effects preclinical
human: Hard-outcome mortality benefit, but only in frail post-fracture patients
safety: Acute flu-like reaction, hypocalcaemia; rare jaw osteonecrosis/atypical fractures
caveats: Mortality data confined to post-fracture cohort; senolytic mechanism preclinical
hallmarks: Cellular senescence; Chronic inflammation; Stem cell exhaustion; Genomic instability
keyStudies: HORIZON-RFT, NEJM 2007 — Annual zoledronate cut all-cause mortality 28% post-hip-fracture [https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa074941] | Samakkarnthai et al., Aging 2023 — Selectively killed senescent cells, lowered SASP, improved grip in aged mice [https://doi.org/10.18632/aging.204701]

name: Urolithin A
mechanism: Induces mitophagy (clearance of damaged mitochondria), improving mitochondrial quality
evidence: One of the better-evidenced novel geroprotectors at the biomarker level: RCTs show improved muscle mitophagy gene expression, ~12% strength/endurance gains, and (2025) shifts toward less-exhausted T cells. Surrogate-only; ~60% of people can't make UA from diet, hence supplementation.
effect: ~10-12% muscle strength/endurance; immune-aging marker shifts
human: Several RCTs on muscle/immune surrogates; no hard outcomes
safety: Well tolerated to 1000 mg/d
caveats: Surrogate-only and partly industry-funded; no lifespan data
hallmarks: Mitochondrial dysfunction; Disabled macroautophagy; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Singh/Liu et al., Cell Rep Med 2022 — ~12% muscle-strength gain, improved endurance & mitophagy markers [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xcrm.2022.100633] | D'Amico et al., Nature Aging 2025 — Reduced markers of immune aging [https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-025-00996-x]

name: MIND Diet
mechanism: Combines Mediterranean + DASH (leafy greens, berries, nuts) to reduce neuroinflammation and vascular damage
evidence: Cohorts linked high adherence to ~35-53% slower cognitive decline, but the definitive 3-year RCT (NEJM 2023) found no cognitive/MRI advantage over a mild-CR control. Strong observational signal not confirmed by RCT; the diet remains healthy and low-risk.
effect: Observational dementia-risk reduction; RCT null on cognition
human: Strong cohort data contradicted by a null definitive RCT
safety: Very safe; nutrient-dense
dose: Daily leafy greens, berries, nuts, whole grains, fish
caveats: Definitive RCT was null; observational benefit likely confounded by healthy lifestyle
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: Barnes et al., NEJM 2023 — No significant cognitive advantage vs control over 3 years [https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2302368] | Morris et al., 2015 (cohort) — ~53% lower Alzheimer's incidence (observational) [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jalz.2014.11.009]

name: Metformin
mechanism: AMPK activation, complex-I inhibition, improved insulin sensitivity, microbiome effects
evidence: Decades of safe use and provocative cohort signals (diabetics on metformin sometimes outliving non-diabetics) motivate the TAME geroprotection trial — still only partially funded. Notably it FAILED to extend lifespan in the ITP and may blunt exercise adaptations.
effect: No lifespan extension in ITP mice; human benefit only shown in diabetics
human: Large diabetes cohorts; TAME RCT pending; unproven in non-diabetics
safety: Very safe; GI upset, B12 depletion, rare lactic acidosis
caveats: May attenuate exercise/muscle gains; geroprotection in healthy people unproven; ITP-negative
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Mitochondrial dysfunction; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Bannister et al., Diab Obes Metab 2014 — Metformin-treated diabetics had lower mortality than matched non-diabetics (confounded) [https://doi.org/10.1111/dom.12354] | MASTERS, Aging Cell 2019 — Metformin blunted resistance-training muscle gains in older adults [https://doi.org/10.1111/acel.13039]

name: Canakinumab
mechanism: Neutralizes IL-1b, blocking a key driver of inflammaging and the senescent-cell SASP
evidence: CANTOS is proof-of-concept that targeting inflammaging improves human outcomes: IL-1b inhibition cut recurrent CV events independent of lipids and reduced lung-cancer mortality. But it did NOT reduce all-cause mortality (fatal infections offset benefits) and is costly/immunosuppressive.
effect: MACE -15%; lung-cancer mortality reduced; all-cause mortality unchanged
human: Hard-outcome RCT validating anti-inflammaging, but no all-cause benefit
safety: Increased fatal infections/sepsis, neutropenia; potent immunosuppression
caveats: No all-cause mortality benefit; infection risk and high cost preclude broad use
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication; Cellular senescence
keyStudies: CANTOS, NEJM 2017 (n=10,061) — MACE HR 0.85; no all-cause mortality benefit; more fatal infections [https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1707914]

name: Magnesium
mechanism: Cofactor for 300+ enzymes incl. ATP metabolism and DNA repair; vascular/neuromuscular regulation
evidence: Strong cohort evidence: each +100 mg/d dietary magnesium associated with ~10% lower all-cause mortality and lower heart-failure/stroke risk. But intake correlates with diet quality, and RCT benefit is concentrated in deficiency/hypertension.
effect: All-cause mortality RR 0.90 (95% CI 0.81-0.99) per 100 mg/d dietary intake; stronger for T2D (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.77-0.86) and stroke (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.89-0.97) — Fang BMC Med 2016 cohort meta-analysis
human: Strong cohort; RCT benefits mainly in deficiency/hypertension
safety: Very safe from food; supplements cause diarrhoea; caution in renal impairment
caveats: Association partly reflects overall diet quality; limited benefit beyond adequacy
hallmarks: Genomic instability; Mitochondrial dysfunction; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Fang et al., BMC Med 2016 — +100 mg/d: all-cause mortality -10%, HF -22% [https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-016-0742-z]

name: Time-Restricted Eating
mechanism: Aligns feeding with circadian rhythm and extends the overnight fast to lower insulin and trigger autophagy
evidence: RCTs and meta-analyses show modest improvements in glucose, weight and BP, largely from incidental calorie reduction; head-to-head it roughly equals plain calorie restriction. A contested (non-peer-reviewed) 2024 analysis linked <8h windows to higher CV mortality.
effect: Small weight/glucose/BP improvements; no demonstrated mortality benefit
human: Many short RCTs on surrogates; mortality data conflicting
safety: Generally well tolerated; caution with diabetes meds, eating disorders
caveats: Benefits largely explained by calorie reduction; one observational analysis suggests possible CV harm
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Altered intercellular communication; Disabled macroautophagy; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Lowe et al., TREAT, JAMA IM 2020 — 16:8 gave no metabolic advantage over 3 meals/day [https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2020.4153]

name: Intermittent Fasting (ADF / 5:2)
mechanism: Recurrent fasts trigger ketogenic switch, autophagy and lowered insulin/IGF-1/mTOR
evidence: Network meta-analyses show all IF forms reduce weight and improve glucose/lipids vs usual diet (alternate-day often largest), but certainty is low and IF roughly equals continuous CR. Benefits appear driven by energy deficit; no hard outcomes.
effect: ~3-8% weight loss; improved insulin sensitivity comparable to CR
human: Numerous RCTs on surrogates; no hard-outcome trials
safety: Hunger, irritability; hypoglycaemia risk on glucose-lowering meds
caveats: Effects largely attributable to calorie deficit; adherence drops; low evidence certainty
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Disabled macroautophagy; Chronic inflammation; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: Trepanowski et al., JAMA IM 2017 — ADF weight loss similar to daily CR, higher dropout [https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2017.0936]

name: Colchicine (low-dose)
mechanism: Binds tubulin to block microtubule assembly, suppressing NLRP3 inflammasome activation and IL-1b/IL-18 release (targets 'inflammaging')
evidence: Two large double-blind RCTs (LoDoCo2 n=5,522; COLCOT n=4,745) show 0.5 mg/day cuts major CV events ~25-31% on top of statins, earning the first FDA approval (2023) of an anti-inflammatory drug for atherosclerotic CVD. But the benefit is non-fatal ischemic events only: NO reduction in CV or all-cause mortality, and pooled data show a significant excess of non-cardiovascular death.
effect: ~25-31% fewer major CV events (pooled OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.60-0.83); no mortality benefit
human: Strong hard-outcome RCT evidence for CV events; no survival benefit shown
safety: Generally tolerated at 0.5 mg/day; signal of excess non-CV death; dangerous with CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors and in renal/hepatic impairment
dose: 0.5 mg orally once daily, added to standard secondary prevention
status: FDA-approved 2023 for CV risk reduction in ASCVD
caveats: Cuts non-fatal events only — no CV or all-cause mortality benefit, and a significant excess of non-cardiovascular deaths in pooled data
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Cellular senescence
keyStudies: Nidorf et al. (LoDoCo2), NEJM 2020 — Primary CV composite HR 0.69 (95% CI 0.57-0.83); non-CV death HR 1.51 (0.99-2.31) [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32865380/] | Akl et al. meta-analysis (8 RCTs, 12,151), 2024 — MACE OR 0.70 (95% CI 0.60-0.83); all-cause mortality OR 1.11 (NS); non-CV death OR 1.54 (1.10-2.15) [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10950412/]

name: Curcumin
mechanism: Pleiotropic anti-inflammatory/antioxidant; inhibits NF-kB/COX-2, modulates Nrf2/AMPK
evidence: Large RCT base shows reductions in CRP, IL-6 and TNF-a and OA pain relief comparable to NSAIDs with bioavailable formulations. No hard-outcome/lifespan data; dismal bioavailability of unformulated curcumin is the key limitation.
effect: CRP reductions; OA pain relief comparable to NSAIDs (formulated)
human: Robust RCT evidence for surrogate/symptomatic outcomes; no longevity endpoints
safety: Very well tolerated; CYP inhibition; rare hepatotoxicity at high dose
caveats: Unformulated curcumin is poorly absorbed; results hinge on formulation — but high-bioavailability/piperine forms are also those linked to a rising number of drug-induced liver-injury cases
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication; Cellular senescence
keyStudies: Curcumin vs diclofenac OA, Trials 2019 — Comparable knee-OA pain relief with fewer GI effects [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30975196/]

name: Aged Garlic Extract / Allicin
mechanism: NO-mediated vasodilation, modest lipid modulation, anti-inflammatory/antiplatelet effects
evidence: Among the better-evidenced botanicals for cardiovascular surrogates: meta-analyses show reductions in systolic BP (~2.5-4 mmHg) and LDL, strongest at >=1200 mg/day and in those with CVD. No powered hard-outcome RCT.
effect: SBP -2.5-4 mmHg (up to ~10 in uncontrolled HTN); small LDL reductions
human: Consistent RCT/meta-analytic evidence for BP/lipids; no hard-outcome RCT
safety: Very safe; garlic odor, GI; antiplatelet (bleeding caution)
caveats: Allicin is unstable; effects require adequate (>=1200 mg) dosing
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: AGE BP/lipid meta-analysis 2025 (19 trials) — SBP -2.5 mmHg, LDL reductions; stronger in CVD [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40628369/]

name: Green Tea (Whole Beverage)
mechanism: Antioxidant/anti-inflammatory polyphenols, endothelial NO support, modest metabolic effects
evidence: Whole-beverage tea has large cohort evidence for lower mortality: a 2024 meta-analysis (38 cohorts, ~1.96M) found highest intake associated with ~10% lower all-cause and ~14% lower CV mortality, plateauing ~2 cups/day. The pooled data cover all tea types (green in Asian, black in European cohorts), not green tea alone. Observational, but the strongest signal among these botanicals — and the beverage avoids EGCG-extract hepatotoxicity.
effect: ~10-15% lower all-cause/CV mortality at highest intake (associative)
human: Strong cohort mortality association; no RCT proving causal lifespan extension
safety: Very safe as a beverage; caffeine effects
caveats: Observational only; the meta-analysis pooled all tea types (not green-specific); benefit is from the beverage, not concentrated extracts
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: Tea & mortality meta-analysis 2024 (38 cohorts) — All-cause HR 0.90, CVD HR 0.86 at highest intake [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11573487/]

name: Blood-Flow Restriction Training
mechanism: Partial venous occlusion during light-load exercise creates metabolic stress driving hypertrophy at low loads
evidence: Meta-analyses show low-load BFR builds strength/hypertrophy comparable to heavy resistance training — valuable for frail/older or injured people who can't lift heavy. Muscle surrogates, not longevity; in some trained groups it is inferior to heavy lifting.
effect: Hypertrophy/strength comparable to heavy lifting at ~20-40% 1RM
human: Robust RCT evidence for muscle; no aging/mortality data
safety: Generally safe done correctly; theoretical clot risk, discomfort, bruising
caveats: An exercise method valuable for those who can't lift heavy, not a validated systemic anti-aging therapy
hallmarks: Stem cell exhaustion; Deregulated nutrient sensing; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Sports Med Open 2024 meta-analysis — Low-load BFR matched high-load training for strength/hypertrophy [https://doi.org/10.1186/s40798-024-00719-3]

name: Glucosamine
mechanism: Cartilage substrate; proposed systemic anti-inflammatory / AMPK (CR-mimetic) effects
evidence: Large cohorts (UK Biobank, ~495k) link regular glucosamine use to ~15% lower all-cause and ~18% lower CV mortality, with mouse data suggesting CR-mimetic effects. All longevity data are observational (healthy-user bias); a dedicated UK Biobank + Mendelian-randomization analysis found glucosamine associated with LOWER incident heart failure (HR ~0.87), so the earlier heart-failure concern is not supported.
effect: All-cause mortality HR 0.85 (95% CI 0.82-0.89), ~15% lower, in regular users; CVD HR 0.82 (95% CI 0.74-0.90) — Li UK Biobank 2020 cohort association, n=495,077
human: Strong cohort associations; no RCT; HF link is protective in MR analysis
safety: Very safe; mild GI; may slightly raise glucose
caveats: All longevity data observational/healthy-user-confounded; no RCT for hard outcomes
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Deregulated nutrient sensing
keyStudies: Li et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2020 (UK Biobank, ~495k) — All-cause mortality HR 0.85; CV HR 0.82 [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7286049/] | Ma et al., Mayo Clin Proc 2023 (UK Biobank + MR) — Glucosamine associated with LOWER incident heart failure (HR 0.87; MR HR 0.92) [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37422736/]

name: Blue Zones / Plant-Forward Pattern
mechanism: Legume/whole-grain/vegetable-rich, low ultra-processed, moderate calories — reduces inflammation and improves the microbiome
evidence: The Blue Zones concept is observational and overlaps with RCT-supported diets (Mediterranean) and Adventist cohorts (vegetarians ~12% lower mortality). But the underlying centenarian demographics face serious data-quality critiques (missing birth records, pension fraud). A hypothesis-generating pattern.
effect: Plant-forward cohorts ~12% lower mortality; Blue Zone magnitude disputed
human: Observational; overlaps with RCT-backed MedDiet; demographics contested
safety: Very safe if well-planned; watch B12/iron/omega-3
dose: Plant-forward whole foods, daily legumes, minimal ultra-processed
caveats: Core longevity claims rest on disputed age records and confounded data
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Dysbiosis; Deregulated nutrient sensing; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Adventist Health Study-2, JAMA IM 2013 — Vegetarian patterns ~12% lower mortality (HR 0.88) [https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2013.6473] | Newman, 2024 (critique) — Many extreme-age records attributable to error/fraud [https://doi.org/10.1101/704080]

name: Meditation / Mindfulness
mechanism: Down-modulates HPA-axis and sympathetic tone, potentially lowering cortisol/inflammation that damage telomeres
evidence: Meta-analyses report small-to-moderate increases in telomerase activity and small reductions in inflammatory markers, but telomere-length effects are weak and the rigorous 18-month Age-Well RCT was null. Stress/well-being benefits are well established; biological-aging effects modest.
effect: Modest telomerase increase; small inflammation reduction; telomere effect inconsistent
human: RCTs on biomarkers/well-being; biological-aging signal weak
safety: Very safe; rare transient anxiety in intensive retreats
status: Established for stress; investigational for aging
caveats: Strongest biological-aging data from confounded long-term-meditator comparisons; RCTs largely null on telomeres
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Telomere attrition; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Schutte & Malouff 2014 — Increased telomerase activity (d~0.46) [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24636500/] | Age-Well RCT 2024 — No significant telomere effect [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bpsgos.2024.100398]

name: Therapeutic Plasma Exchange
mechanism: Removing plasma and replacing with albumin dilutes pro-aging circulating factors, shifting the proteome younger
evidence: The AMBAR Phase 2b/3 RCT (n~347) in Alzheimer's found TPE with albumin slowed cognitive/functional decline vs sham — the strongest controlled evidence for any plasma-based aging-adjacent intervention. Effect was modest and disease-specific; biological-age data are preliminary.
effect: Slowed AD progression (modest, disease-specific); biological-age reduction reported in small study
human: One large RCT (Alzheimer's) + small biomarker studies; no general-aging RCT
safety: Generally well tolerated; hypotension, citrate reactions, line/infection risks
dose: AMBAR: weekly x6 then monthly x12 months
caveats: Best RCT is in Alzheimer's with modest effect; general anti-aging benefit hypothesis-driven
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation; Cellular senescence
keyStudies: Boada et al., Alz & Dementia 2020 (AMBAR) — Slowed decline in moderate Alzheimer's vs sham [https://alz-journals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/alz.12137]

name: Spermidine
mechanism: Induces autophagy, promoting cellular renewal and proteostasis
evidence: Best human evidence is observational: cohorts link higher dietary spermidine to lower all-cause/CV mortality. But the key RCT (SmartAge) was NULL — 12 months did not improve memory or biomarkers. Strong animal autophagy/lifespan data; human causal benefit unproven.
effect: Strong cohort mortality association; RCT showed no cognitive effect
human: Strong cohort signal but rigorous RCT was null
safety: Well tolerated; no notable adverse effects
caveats: Cohort data likely confounded by diet quality; the one good RCT failed its endpoint
hallmarks: Disabled macroautophagy; Loss of proteostasis; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Kiechl et al., AJCN 2018 (Bruneck) — Higher intake linked to markedly lower mortality [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29955838/] | SmartAge RCT, JAMA Netw Open 2022 — NULL on memory/biomarkers at tested dose [https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2022.13875]

name: N-Acetylcysteine (NAC)
mechanism: Cysteine/glutathione precursor; replenishes glutathione, scavenges ROS
evidence: Solid disease-specific evidence (reduces COPD exacerbations; acetaminophen antidote), but aging-specific human data are confined to glutathione/oxidative surrogates and to GlyNAC. Mouse lifespan data come within GlyNAC.
effect: COPD exacerbation reduction; aging effects surrogate-level
human: Strong for COPD/overdose; aging benefit mostly as GlyNAC component
safety: Very safe orally; antioxidants may blunt some exercise adaptations
status: Rx drug + OTC supplement (US status contested)
caveats: Standalone anti-aging benefit unproven
hallmarks: Loss of proteostasis; Mitochondrial dysfunction; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: COPD meta-analyses — ~10-25% fewer COPD exacerbations [https://doi.org/10.1183/16000617.00002215]

name: Selenium
mechanism: Incorporated into selenoproteins (glutathione peroxidases) for antioxidant defense
evidence: A cautionary U-shaped nutrient: the large SELECT RCT (n=35,533) found selenium did not prevent cancer. The statistically significant prostate-cancer increase in SELECT came from vitamin E, not selenium (selenium alone HR 1.09, NS); a diabetes signal with selenium comes mainly from the earlier NPC trial. Benefit appears confined to deficiency (e.g. with CoQ10 in KiSel-10); supplementing the replete is neutral.
effect: No cancer-prevention benefit; benefit largely confined to deficiency
human: Large RCT (SELECT) shows no cancer-prevention benefit; harms with selenium alone were non-significant
safety: Narrow window; frank excess causes selenosis; a diabetes signal seen in some trials (NPC); high-dose caution
dose: ~55 ug/day RDA; avoid high-dose if replete
status: OTC mineral (flagged for harm in repletion)
caveats: Beneficial mainly in deficiency; high-dose carries selenosis/diabetes concern. Note: the significant prostate-cancer harm in SELECT was from vitamin E, not selenium.
hallmarks: Genomic instability; Chronic inflammation; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: SELECT, JAMA 2011 (n=35,533) — No cancer prevention; selenium alone NS for prostate cancer (HR 1.09); the significant increase was from vitamin E (HR 1.17) [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4169010/] | Alehagen et al., KiSel-10 — Selenium+CoQ10 cut CV mortality in selenium-deficient elderly [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22626835/]

name: Berberine
mechanism: AMPK activation with downstream effects on gluconeogenesis, lipogenesis and autophagy
evidence: Among botanicals this has strong mechanistic plausibility (genuine AMPK activator) and good human metabolic RCT data — meaningful reductions in fasting glucose, HbA1c, triglycerides and LDL, with glucose-lowering approaching metformin. Surrogate-only; bioavailability poor.
effect: HbA1c ~-0.5-0.8% (up to ~1% at high baseline); meaningful lipid reductions
human: Good RCT/meta-analytic evidence for metabolic surrogates; no hard outcomes
safety: GI effects in ~20-35%; potent CYP3A4/2D6 inhibitor (interactions); avoid in pregnancy
caveats: Poor bioavailability and notable drug interactions; metabolic adjunct, not metformin replacement
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Disabled macroautophagy; Chronic inflammation; Dysbiosis
keyStudies: T2D meta-analysis 2022 — Reduced FBG/HbA1c comparably to metformin [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36467075/]

name: Fasting-Mimicking Diet
mechanism: 5-day low-cal/low-protein cycles mimic water-fast physiology — downregulate IGF-1/mTOR, induce autophagy and post-cycle regeneration
evidence: Longo's group reported 3-4 monthly FMD cycles lowered estimated biological age ~2.5 years and improved insulin resistance/liver fat across two cohorts. Surrogate (biological-age) endpoints, short-term, from groups with commercial interest; no hard outcomes.
effect: ~2.5-year reduction in estimated biological age; improved metabolic markers
human: Small RCTs/cohorts on biomarkers; industry-affiliated
safety: Generally well tolerated; transient fatigue/hunger; caution in diabetes/frailty
caveats: Biomarker-only endpoints, short follow-up, sponsor involvement; durability unproven
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Disabled macroautophagy; Stem cell exhaustion; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Brandhorst/Longo, Nat Commun 2024 — 3-4 FMD cycles reduced biological age ~2.5 yr [https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-45260-9]

name: Low-dose Aspirin
mechanism: Irreversibly inhibits COX-1/2, reducing thromboxane/prostaglandins (antiplatelet, anti-inflammatory)
evidence: A cautionary translation failure: a modest ITP mouse signal but the large ASPREE RCT found no benefit and numerically HIGHER all-cause mortality (cancer deaths) plus more major bleeding in healthy older adults.
effect: Net harm in healthy elderly (all-cause HR ~1.14)
human: Negative/harmful for primary prevention; benefit only in secondary prevention
safety: Major risk is GI/intracranial haemorrhage
status: OTC; not supported for healthy-aging prevention
caveats: Animal-to-human translation failure; net harm in healthy elderly
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: ASPREE, NEJM 2018 (n=19,114) — No disability-free-survival benefit; all-cause mortality HR 1.14; more haemorrhage [https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1800722] | Strong et al., ITP 2008 — +8% male mouse median lifespan [https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1474-9726.2008.00414.x]

name: GlyNAC (Glycine + NAC)
mechanism: Supplies both glutathione precursors, restoring redox, mitochondrial function and lowering inflammation
evidence: Baylor (Sekhar) RCTs in older adults show GlyNAC corrects glutathione deficiency and improves a broad panel of aging surrogates (oxidative stress, inflammation, insulin resistance, gait, strength). But trials are small, single-lab and biomarker-based; mouse lifespan +24%.
effect: Large improvements in oxidative-stress/inflammation/insulin-resistance surrogates
human: Promising small RCTs; needs large independent replication
safety: Well tolerated; high amino-acid load
caveats: Small single-lab studies with dramatic biomarker claims; effects likely shrink in larger trials
hallmarks: Mitochondrial dysfunction; Loss of proteostasis; Chronic inflammation; Deregulated nutrient sensing
keyStudies: Kumar et al., J Gerontol 2023 RCT — Improved glutathione, oxidative stress, gait, strength, cognition vs placebo [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9879756/]

name: Sulforaphane
mechanism: Activates Keap1-Nrf2-ARE, inducing endogenous antioxidant/detox enzymes
evidence: The prototypical dietary Nrf2 activator with many small RCTs showing reproducible Nrf2-target induction, lowered fasting glucose/HbA1c in diabetics (via reduced hepatic glucose output), and lower inflammatory markers. Results are biomarker-level and variable; bioavailability depends heavily on formulation.
effect: Modest glycaemic and oxidative/inflammatory improvements; reliable Nrf2 induction
human: Many small RCTs on surrogates
safety: Generally safe; GI upset; bioavailability varies hugely
caveats: Highly variable bioavailability; no longevity outcome data despite strong mechanism
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Genomic instability; Loss of proteostasis
keyStudies: Axelsson et al., Sci Transl Med 2017 — Lowered fasting glucose/HbA1c in type-2 diabetes [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28615356/]

name: Ergothioneine
mechanism: Cytoprotective antioxidant accumulated via a dedicated transporter in high-stress tissues
evidence: A proposed 'longevity vitamin' (humans have a dedicated transporter). Strongest data are cohort — higher plasma ergothioneine predicted lower CV and all-cause mortality over 21 years. Compelling but observational; intervention evidence only early-stage.
effect: All-cause mortality ~-14% per SD (cohort)
human: Strong cohort/mechanistic case; intervention RCTs early-stage
safety: Appears very safe; accumulates selectively
caveats: Mortality data associational; whether supplementing replicates the cohort benefit is unproven
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Mitochondrial dysfunction; Genomic instability
keyStudies: Smith et al., Heart 2019 (Malmo) — Higher plasma EGT: all-cause mortality HR ~0.86 over 21 yr [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7229907/]

name: Collagen Peptides
mechanism: Provides glycine/proline + bioactive peptides that may signal fibroblast collagen synthesis
evidence: For skin aging the evidence is reasonably solid: meta-analyses of RCTs find ~3 months improves skin hydration, elasticity and wrinkles; joint data are positive but variable. Many trials are industry-funded; endpoints cosmetic/functional, not longevity.
effect: Measurable skin elasticity/hydration gains; modest joint relief
human: Multiple positive RCTs on skin; weaker on joints
safety: Very safe
caveats: Mostly cosmetic surrogates and industry-funded; no evidence it affects systemic aging
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Stem cell exhaustion
keyStudies: Skin-aging meta-analysis, Am J Med 2025 — Improved hydration, elasticity, fewer wrinkles vs placebo [https://www.amjmed.com/article/S0002-9343(25)00283-9/abstract]

name: Acarbose
mechanism: Blunts post-prandial glucose spikes by slowing carbohydrate digestion (CR-mimetic)
evidence: One of the most reproducible ITP hits, with a striking male-biased lifespan extension confirmed across doses and sites. Combined with rapamycin it produced one of the largest ITP effects on record. No human longevity data.
effect: +22% male median lifespan (mice, ITP)
human: No human longevity trial; glycemic surrogate data only
safety: Metabolically well tolerated; dose-dependent flatulence/diarrhea limit adherence
caveats: Robust in mice but male-specific; zero human lifespan data; GI side effects
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Harrison et al., Aging Cell 2014 (ITP) — +22% male / +5% female median lifespan [https://doi.org/10.1111/acel.12170] | Strong et al., Aging Cell 2022 (ITP) — Rapamycin+acarbose ~+37% male median lifespan [https://doi.org/10.1111/acel.13724]

name: Canagliflozin
mechanism: Blocks renal glucose reabsorption, inducing a mild fasting-like metabolic state
evidence: An ITP success in males — extended male mouse lifespan and delayed tumours, with no female lifespan effect. The SGLT2 class has strong human CV/kidney mortality data, but canagliflozin specifically carries an amputation-risk signal.
effect: +14% male median lifespan (mice, ITP)
human: No longevity RCT; class CV/renal mortality benefit in disease
safety: Genital infections, volume depletion, euglycemic DKA; amputation/fracture signal unique to canagliflozin
caveats: Male-only mouse benefit; amputation signal makes other SGLT2i safer; no human aging data
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Miller et al., ITP 2020 — +14% male median lifespan; no female effect; delayed neoplasia [https://doi.org/10.1172/jci.insight.140019] | CANVAS, NEJM 2017 — Lower MACE but ~2x amputation risk in diabetics [https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1611925]

name: Alpha-Lipoic Acid
mechanism: Universal antioxidant; regenerates other antioxidants; mitochondrial cofactor; AMPK effects
evidence: Best evidence is for diabetic neuropathy (symptom improvement short-term), though the long-term NATHAN-1 RCT missed its primary endpoint. Other RCTs show reduced oxidative markers and modest metabolic improvement. Aging-specific data absent.
effect: Symptomatic neuropathy improvement; modest metabolic effects
human: RCTs in neuropathy/metabolic disease; no aging data
safety: Generally safe; can lower glucose; rare insulin-autoimmune syndrome
caveats: Evidence is disease-specific, not longevity; flagship neuropathy RCT missed its primary endpoint
hallmarks: Mitochondrial dysfunction; Chronic inflammation; Deregulated nutrient sensing
keyStudies: Ziegler et al., NATHAN-1, Diab Care 2011 — Missed primary endpoint; improved some neuropathy measures [https://diabetesjournals.org/care/article/34/9/2054/38685/]

name: Infrared Sauna
mechanism: Lower-temperature radiant heat raises core temperature, improving endothelial function and cardiac output
evidence: Best evidence is the Japanese Waon-therapy program in chronic heart failure — small RCTs show improved cardiac function, exercise tolerance and lower BNP. Surrogate/functional endpoints in disease populations, mostly from one research group; no healthy-population longevity data.
effect: CHF: improved ejection fraction/BNP/6-min walk; healthy longevity effect unknown
human: RCTs positive in heart failure; no healthy-population longevity data
safety: Generally safe; lower thermal load than traditional sauna
caveats: Most positive data from one group in heart-failure patients; consumer units differ from clinical Waon
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Tei/Kihara, Waon therapy (CHF) — Improved cardiac function and exercise tolerance in CHF [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11869837/]

name: Senolytics: Dasatinib + Quercetin
mechanism: Transiently kills senescent cells by disabling their pro-survival pathways
evidence: The best-validated senolytic combination in humans, but evidence is early-phase and mostly on biomarkers/feasibility. Small trials show reduced senescent-cell burden (diabetic kidney disease) and improved physical function (IPF); a 2025 Alzheimer's pilot was single-arm. No placebo-controlled hard-outcome win yet.
effect: Large in mice (healthspan); human clinical benefit unproven
human: Small early-phase RCTs; target engagement shown, efficacy not
safety: Dasatinib (a chemo drug) carries cytopenias, effusions, bleeding risk; intermittent dosing
caveats: Dasatinib is a real chemo agent; no placebo-controlled hard-outcome win; DIY use hazardous
hallmarks: Cellular senescence; Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Hickson et al., EBioMedicine 2019 — 3-day D+Q reduced senescent-cell markers and SASP in patients [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6796530/] | Justice et al., EBioMedicine 2019 — Improved 6-min walk/gait in small IPF pilot [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2352396418306297]

name: Vitamin K2 (MK-7)
mechanism: Carboxylates matrix-Gla protein (inhibits vascular calcification) and osteocalcin (bone)
evidence: Strong observational case (Rotterdam Study linked high intake to ~50% lower aortic calcification and ~25% lower all-cause mortality), with a well-established mechanism — but RCTs have been largely null on hard calcification/clinical endpoints.
effect: Large cohort associations; RCTs mostly null on hard endpoints
human: Strong observational + mechanism, but RCTs underwhelming
safety: Very safe; interacts with warfarin
caveats: 'Reverses arterial calcification' claims rest on cohorts/surrogates; RCTs have largely failed to confirm
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Geleijnse et al., Rotterdam Study — Highest K2 intake: ~25% lower all-cause mortality [https://doi.org/10.1093/jn/134.11.3100] | K2+D aortic-valve RCT, Circulation 2022 — No significant slowing of calcification [https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.121.057008]

name: Silymarin (Milk Thistle)
mechanism: Hepatoprotective antioxidant; reduces lipid peroxidation and inflammation in liver
evidence: Best evidence is for liver biomarkers: meta-analyses show silymarin lowers transaminases and improves liver fat in NAFLD/NASH. Surrogate (enzymes/imaging), not histological hard outcomes; bioavailability poor. A liver-targeted, not general-longevity, agent.
effect: ALT/AST reductions; modest liver-fat improvement
human: Good RCT/meta evidence for liver surrogates; no hard-outcome data
safety: Very well tolerated; mild GI; CYP/UGT interactions
caveats: Poor bioavailability; benefit is liver-specific, not systemic anti-aging
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Mitochondrial dysfunction; Genomic instability
keyStudies: NAFLD meta-analysis 2024 (26 trials) — Improved liver enzymes and hepatic fat [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aohep.2023.101174]

name: NR (Nicotinamide Riboside)
mechanism: Converted via NMN to NAD+, supporting sirtuin/PARP/mitochondrial function
evidence: The best-studied NAD+ precursor in humans — dependably raises NAD+, but clinical benefits are limited and inconsistent and it did NOT extend lifespan in the rigorous ITP. The NICE trial improved 6-min walk only modestly; other trials were largely null.
effect: Reliably raises NAD+; small/mostly-null clinical effects; no mouse lifespan extension
human: Many RCTs confirming NAD+ rise and safety; benefits modest/heterogeneous
safety: Very good; safe up to 2 g/day in trials
caveats: Did NOT extend lifespan in the gold-standard ITP; biomarker change != healthspan benefit
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Mitochondrial dysfunction; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: NICE trial, Nat Commun 2024 — 1000 mg/d improved 6-min walk +17.6 m (small) [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11176364/] | NIA ITP 2021 — NR did not extend mouse lifespan [https://doi.org/10.1111/acel.13328]

name: Melatonin
mechanism: Circadian regulator; potent mitochondrial antioxidant and anti-inflammatory
evidence: Strong for sleep-onset/circadian use and a good mitochondrial antioxidant, but longevity 'mortality benefit' claims rest on animal/mechanistic data. New 2025 cohort data link long-term use to higher heart-failure and mortality — possibly confounding, but it tempers the 'safe longevity supplement' narrative.
effect: Reliable for sleep latency; mortality effect unproven and possibly adverse
human: Good for sleep; longevity benefit unproven, 2025 safety signal
safety: Short-term very safe; 2025 data flag possible HF/mortality association with chronic use
status: OTC (US); Rx in much of EU/UK
caveats: Hyped as anti-aging antioxidant, but human longevity evidence weak and a 2025 safety question exists
hallmarks: Mitochondrial dysfunction; Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: AHA 2025 cohort — Long-term use linked to ~89% higher incident HF and ~2x mortality (observational) [https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/circ.152.suppl_3.4371606]

name: Ashwagandha
mechanism: HPA-axis modulation lowering cortisol; GABAergic/serotonergic and antioxidant effects
evidence: One of the better-supported adaptogens for stress: meta-analyses of ~15 RCTs show significant reductions in perceived stress, anxiety and cortisol. Short-term and symptom/biomarker based; no aging/lifespan outcomes.
effect: Perceived-stress and cortisol reductions
human: Good short-term RCT evidence for stress/anxiety; no longevity endpoints
safety: Generally well tolerated short term; a recognized idiosyncratic cholestatic liver-injury signal (rare, incl. isolated acute liver failure); may affect thyroid; caution in autoimmune/pregnancy
caveats: Perceived-stress benefit is contested across 2025 meta-analyses (cortisol reduction more consistent); a documented idiosyncratic liver-injury signal; extract heterogeneity
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: Stress/anxiety meta-analysis, BJPsych Open 2025 — Reduced Perceived Stress Scale, HAM-A and serum cortisol [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12242034/]

name: Oleuropein / Olive Leaf Extract
mechanism: NO-mediated vasodilation and antioxidant signaling; modest insulin-sensitizing effects
evidence: RCT meta-analyses show olive leaf extract lowers systolic BP (~4-5 mmHg) and triglycerides; olive polyphenol (hydroxytyrosol) carries an EFSA claim for LDL-oxidation protection. Surrogate endpoints; no hard-outcome RCT.
effect: SBP -4-5 mmHg; triglyceride reductions
human: RCT/meta evidence for BP/lipid surrogates; no hard-outcome data
safety: Very well tolerated; additive with antihypertensives
caveats: Glucose effects inconsistent; oleuropein content varies
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation; Deregulated nutrient sensing
keyStudies: OLE CV meta-analysis 2022 (12 studies) — SBP -3.9 mmHg; in hypertensives SBP -4.8 mmHg [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9585795/]

name: Red Light Therapy / Photobiomodulation
mechanism: Red/near-infrared photons absorbed by cytochrome c oxidase boost mitochondrial ATP and modulate inflammation
evidence: The mechanism is well established, and human RCTs support specific dermatologic (wrinkles, wound healing) and musculoskeletal pain endpoints. An umbrella review found benefits across outcomes but rated certainty low-to-moderate with non-standardized protocols; no aging/lifespan outcomes.
effect: Outcome-specific: skin rejuvenation, wound healing, some pain
human: Multiple RCTs for surrogate endpoints; nothing on aging/lifespan
safety: Very safe for skin; eye protection needed; dose-response is biphasic
status: FDA-cleared for specific indications; broad anti-aging claims unproven
caveats: Strong mechanism but longevity claims extrapolate from surrogate/in-vitro data; protocols not standardized
hallmarks: Mitochondrial dysfunction; Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Umbrella review, Syst Rev 2025 — Improved pain/skin/mucositis outcomes; certainty low-to-moderate [https://doi.org/10.1186/s13643-025-02902-3]

name: Whole-Body Vibration
mechanism: Mechanical accelerations stimulate reflexive muscle contraction and bone mechanotransduction
evidence: Meta-analyses in older adults show modest, region-specific bone-density gains and improved strength/balance/fall measures, but effects are inconsistent across skeletal sites. No mortality or systemic aging outcomes.
effect: Small site-specific BMD gains; modest strength/balance improvement
human: RCTs positive for BMD/strength surrogates; no longevity data
safety: Generally safe; caution with thrombosis, recent fractures, pregnancy
caveats: Benefits modest, site-dependent, limited to musculoskeletal surrogates
hallmarks: Stem cell exhaustion; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: WBV meta-analysis 2026 (1,447 older adults) — BMD gains at trochanter/Ward's; inconsistent at femoral neck/spine across meta-analyses [https://doi.org/10.1186/s12891-026-09504-7]

name: Ginkgo Biloba
mechanism: Improves microcirculation/cerebral blood flow; antioxidant; PAF antagonism
evidence: For treating existing mild dementia, EGb 761 at 240 mg/day shows benefits on cognition and function. But for prevention it FAILED: the large GEM and GuidAge trials showed it does not prevent dementia in healthy older adults. A symptomatic agent, not a prevention/longevity tool.
effect: Modest symptomatic benefit in established dementia; no preventive benefit
human: Positive for treating dementia, clearly negative for prevention
