safety: Generally well tolerated; antiplatelet/bleeding risk
caveats: Does not prevent dementia/aging despite popular belief; bleeding risk
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: GEM Study, JAMA 2008 — Did NOT reduce incidence of dementia/Alzheimer's [https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2008.683] | GuidAge, Lancet Neurol 2012 (n>2,800) — Long-term EGb 761 did NOT prevent Alzheimer's in elders with memory complaints [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22959217/] | EGb 761 mild-dementia meta-analysis — 240 mg/d superior to placebo for cognition/ADL [https://doi.org/10.1080/15622975.2024.2446830]

name: Saffron (Crocin)
mechanism: Serotonergic/dopaminergic modulation; antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects
evidence: A relatively strong RCT base for mood: 20+ RCTs and meta-analyses show large effects for depression and anxiety, comparable to SSRIs with fewer adverse events. Endpoints are psychiatric scales, not aging; trials mostly short and group-clustered.
effect: Clinically meaningful antidepressant/anxiolytic effect
human: Good RCT/meta evidence for mood; no longevity data
safety: Well tolerated at supplement doses; high doses (>1.5 g) toxic; avoid in pregnancy
caveats: Dose-toxicity margin and frequent adulteration; trials short/group-clustered
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: Depression/anxiety meta-analysis — Large effect vs placebo (g~0.99); comparable to SSRIs [https://academic.oup.com/nutritionreviews/article/77/8/557/5499264]

name: Bacopa Monnieri
mechanism: Cholinergic modulation, dendritic/synaptic effects, hippocampal antioxidant action
evidence: Meta-analyses with chronic (>=12 week) dosing show improved cognition, especially attention speed and memory; ranks among top botanicals for executive function in older adults. Effects modest, require sustained dosing; cognitive surrogates only.
effect: Small improvements in attention speed and memory
human: Multiple RCTs for cognitive surrogates; no longevity data
safety: Generally well tolerated; dose-related GI effects common
caveats: Requires weeks of dosing; GI side effects; modest effect sizes
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication; Genomic instability
keyStudies: Bacopa cognition meta-analysis — Improved speed of attention with chronic dosing [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24252493/]

name: DHEA
mechanism: Adrenal prohormone converted to androgens/estrogens; weak direct receptor activity
evidence: RCTs and a meta-analysis show at most small, sex-specific effects (modest BMD gain in older women, slight body-composition changes in men) and no consistent benefit for muscle, cognition or well-being. No mortality or anti-aging endpoint met despite age-related decline of DHEA-S.
effect: Small lumbar-spine BMD gain in women; minor body-composition shifts; no longevity effect
human: Multiple RCTs; marginal sex-specific benefits
safety: Generally tolerated at 50 mg/d; androgenic effects; theoretical hormone-sensitive cancer concern
caveats: Popular as anti-aging but evidence shows only marginal surrogate benefits and no survival effect
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Stem cell exhaustion
keyStudies: Corona et al., JCEM 2013 meta-analysis — Small body-composition gain in men; no clear clinical benefit [https://doi.org/10.1210/jc.2013-1358] | Weiss/Villareal DHEA-bone RCTs (50 mg/d) — Modest lumbar-spine BMD gain in older women; no bone benefit in men [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19321570/]

name: NMN
mechanism: Converted to NAD+ to support sirtuins, DNA repair and mitochondrial metabolism
evidence: Reliably raises blood NAD+ and a few small RCTs report modest functional signals (walking speed, aerobic capacity), but evidence is limited, mixed and surrogate. No hard-outcome or lifespan data; NMN was never tested in the ITP (its relative NR was, and failed).
effect: Reliably raises NAD+; modest, inconsistent functional gains
human: Several small short RCTs (surrogate endpoints)
safety: Well tolerated up to 1200 mg/d short-term; long-term unknown
caveats: Raising NAD+ does not prove longevity benefit; trials small/short; US status contested
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Mitochondrial dysfunction; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Igarashi et al., 2024 RCT — 250 mg/d x12wk maintained walking speed (vs decline on placebo) and improved sleep in older adults [https://doi.org/10.1007/s11357-024-01204-1] | Liao et al., 2021 RCT — Dose-dependent aerobic-capacity gains in runners [https://doi.org/10.1186/s12970-021-00442-4]

name: Niacin (Nicotinic Acid)
mechanism: Salvaged to NAD+ (Preiss-Handler); activates GPR109A (flushing); modifies lipids
evidence: Striking NAD+-restoration in a rare disease (mitochondrial myopathy) — niacin normalized muscle NAD+ and improved strength. But as a lipid drug, large CV outcome trials (HPS2-THRIVE) found no benefit and more harm, and a metabolite (4PY) may raise CV risk. 'More niacin' is not benign.
effect: Disease-specific NAD+ rescue; null/harmful for general CV prevention at high dose
human: Strong in a niche deficiency disease; harmful in large CV trials
safety: Marked flushing; high doses cause hepatotoxicity, hyperglycaemia, gout; CV harm signal
caveats: NAD+ rescue specific to mitochondrial myopathy; high-dose niacin failed/harmed in CV trials
hallmarks: Mitochondrial dysfunction; Deregulated nutrient sensing; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Pirinen et al., Cell Metab 2020 — Restored muscle NAD+ and strength in mitochondrial myopathy [https://www.cell.com/cell-metabolism/fulltext/S1550-4131(20)30190-X] | HPS2-THRIVE, NEJM 2014 — No CV benefit, increased adverse effects (>25,000 patients) [https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1300955]

name: Carnosine / L-Carnosine
mechanism: Anti-glycation carbonyl scavenger, pH buffer, antioxidant, metal chelator
evidence: Mechanistically attractive anti-glycation dipeptide. RCTs (2 g/d) show improved glycaemic control and some cognitive-speed gains, but cognitive benefit appeared only in the youngest subgroup; rapidly degraded by serum carnosinase (bioavailability issue).
effect: Modest glycaemic improvement; age-dependent cognitive effect
human: Small RCTs on glycaemia/cognition; bioavailability-limited
safety: Well tolerated at gram doses
caveats: Serum carnosinase rapidly degrades oral carnosine; benefits small and not shown for aging in older adults
hallmarks: Loss of proteostasis; Chronic inflammation; Cellular senescence
keyStudies: de Courten et al. RCT — Improved glucose control in pre-diabetes/T2DM [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.numecd.2023.10.012]

name: Hesperidin
mechanism: Improves endothelial function and NO bioavailability; anti-inflammatory/antioxidant
evidence: A 2023 dose-response meta-analysis (13 RCTs) found hesperidin significantly lowers LDL (~5 mg/dL); fasting glucose and CRP were non-significant overall (positive only in subgroups), and adhesion molecules were not assessed. Endothelial/FMD improvement (~2-2.5%) is seen in separate small RCTs. Surrogate endpoints; bioavailability poor and microbiome-dependent.
effect: Modest LDL reduction; improved FMD in small RCTs; glucose/inflammation effects inconsistent
human: Meta-analysis shows LDL reduction; glucose/CRP null overall; no longevity data
safety: Very well tolerated; additive with antihypertensives
caveats: Low/variable bioavailability dependent on gut microbiota
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Cardiometabolic meta-analysis, Front Nutr 2023 (13 RCTs) — LDL -5.3 mg/dL (significant); fasting glucose and CRP non-significant overall [https://doi.org/10.3389/fnut.2023.1177708] | Citrus/orange-juice RCTs — Improved FMD ~2-2.5% in elevated-BP subjects

name: Cold Exposure / Cold-Water Immersion
mechanism: Cold activates brown fat and mitochondrial biogenesis, raises norepinephrine and improves insulin sensitivity
evidence: Small trials show cold activates brown fat, raises energy expenditure and insulin sensitivity (~40% in one mild-cold protocol); norepinephrine/mood effects are reproducible. No human longevity evidence, and acute immersion carries real cardiovascular and drowning risk.
effect: Insulin sensitivity +~40% (mild cold); large transient norepinephrine surge
human: Surrogate/metabolic RCTs; no longevity/hard-outcome data
safety: Acute cold-shock, arrhythmia, drowning, post-immersion hypotension; dangerous with cardiac disease
dose: ~10-15 min/wk cumulative at ~10-15C, or short plunges
caveats: Metabolic effects real but small/short-lived; no human longevity evidence and non-trivial acute danger
hallmarks: Mitochondrial dysfunction; Deregulated nutrient sensing; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: van der Lans et al., JCI 2013 — 10 days mild cold improved insulin sensitivity ~43% and recruited brown fat [https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI68993]

name: NR + Pterostilbene
mechanism: NR raises NAD+ while pterostilbene is proposed to activate sirtuins (synergy unproven)
evidence: Reliably raises NAD+ and is safe, but human clinical benefit is weak and synergy unproven — the pivotal NAFLD RCT MISSED its primary endpoint (no change in liver fat).
effect: Reliable NAD+ rise; weak/subset-only functional signals; primary NAFLD endpoint negative
human: Several RCTs; safe but mostly null clinical outcomes
safety: Well tolerated
caveats: Heavily marketed but pivotal trial missed its primary endpoint; pterostilbene's added benefit unproven
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Mitochondrial dysfunction; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Dellinger et al., Hepatology 2023 — NRPT missed primary NAFLD endpoint (hepatic fat unchanged) [https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/hep.32778]

name: Glycine
mechanism: Glutathione precursor; one-carbon/methionine modulation; possible methionine-restriction mimetic
evidence: Promising animal data — glycine modestly extended median lifespan in the ITP and in worms. Human data limited to short-term metabolic/sleep endpoints and to its role within GlyNAC; no standalone longevity trials.
effect: Modest mouse median-lifespan extension; human effects metabolic/sleep only
human: No human longevity trials
safety: Very safe; GI upset at high doses
caveats: Most aging evidence animal/mechanistic or bundled with NAC
hallmarks: Loss of proteostasis; Mitochondrial dysfunction; Deregulated nutrient sensing
keyStudies: NIA ITP 2019 — Small but significant median-lifespan increase in mice [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30916479/]

name: Taurine
mechanism: Osmolyte/antioxidant supporting mitochondria, calcium handling and reduced senescence
evidence: A 2023 Science paper showed taurine extended mouse lifespan ~10-12% and improved healthspan in mice/monkeys — but a 2025 NIH follow-up found taurine does NOT decline with age in humans/monkeys/mice, undercutting the core premise. No human lifespan RCT.
effect: ~+10-12% mouse lifespan; human longevity effect unknown
human: No human lifespan RCT; 2025 data question the rationale
safety: Very safe at gram doses
caveats: High-profile 2023 result contested by 2025 human/primate data — strong hype-vs-evidence gap
hallmarks: Mitochondrial dysfunction; Cellular senescence; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Singh et al., Science 2023 — +10-12% mouse median lifespan; healthspan gains [https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abn9257] | Fernandez et al., Science 2025 — Taurine does not decline with age in humans/primates (contests biomarker premise) [https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adl2116]

name: Panax Ginseng
mechanism: Ginsenoside effects on CNS, anti-fatigue, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant signaling
evidence: Meta-analyses suggest modest benefits for cognition and fatigue, with small trials showing improved memory and reduced stress. Trials are heterogeneous in preparation/dose; outcomes are cognitive/symptom surrogates with no longevity data.
effect: Modest cognitive and anti-fatigue effects
human: Multiple RCTs for cognition/fatigue surrogates; no longevity data
safety: Generally safe; insomnia, headache; may lower glucose; warfarin interaction
caveats: Heterogeneous preparations and modest effect sizes
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: Cognition meta-analysis, Phytother Res 2024 — Improves aspects of cognitive function vs control [https://doi.org/10.1002/ptr.8359]

name: Protein / Methionine Restriction
mechanism: Lowering protein/methionine downregulates mTORC1 and IGF-1, shifting toward stress resistance and autophagy
evidence: Methionine restriction robustly extends lifespan in rodents/flies. Short human trials lower IGF-1/LDL, and cohorts link high protein in midlife to higher mortality but the OPPOSITE after 65. Strongly age-dependent; no human lifespan RCT.
effect: Animal lifespan +30-40% (methionine restriction); human surrogate/age-stratified signals
human: Short metabolic trials + cohorts; no lifespan RCT; age-dependent
safety: Risk of sarcopenia/frailty, esp. in elderly; hard to achieve without near-vegan diet
caveats: Strongly age-dependent — beneficial midlife but harmful (sarcopenia) in older adults
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Disabled macroautophagy; Cellular senescence; Loss of proteostasis
keyStudies: Levine et al., Cell Metab 2014 (NHANES) — High protein at 50-65 linked to higher mortality; reversed after 65 [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cmet.2014.02.006]

name: Ketogenic Diet
mechanism: Carb restriction shifts fuel to ketones (BHB, an HDAC inhibitor/signaling molecule)
evidence: Longevity evidence is mixed/weak: one NHANES analysis linked a higher ketogenic ratio to ~24% lower mortality, yet other cohorts find animal-based very-low-carb associated with HIGHER mortality, and keto often raises LDL. Mouse cyclic-keto reduced midlife mortality. No long-term human RCT for lifespan.
effect: Mixed: one cohort -24% mortality; others higher; LDL often rises
human: Conflicting cohort data; no lifespan RCT
safety: LDL elevation in many; keto flu, nutrient gaps; fat source matters
caveats: Longevity evidence contradictory; CV safety depends heavily on fat source
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Mitochondrial dysfunction; Chronic inflammation; Epigenetic alterations
keyStudies: Newman et al., Cell Metab 2017 (mice) — Cyclic keto reduced midlife mortality and improved memory in aging mice [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cmet.2017.08.004] | Roberts et al., Cell Metab 2017 (mice) — Continuous keto extended median lifespan and preserved function in adult mice [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cmet.2017.08.005] | Seidelmann et al., Lancet PH 2018 — U-shaped carb-mortality; animal-based low-carb worse [https://doi.org/10.1016/S2468-2667(18)30135-X]

name: Contrast Therapy (Hot-Cold)
mechanism: Alternating vasodilation/vasoconstriction acts as a vascular pump and modulates autonomic tone
evidence: Meta-analyses in athletes show contrast therapy reduces muscle soreness/strength loss better than passive rest, but not clearly better than cold-water immersion. Evidence is confined to short-term exercise recovery; no aging/healthspan data.
effect: Moderate reduction in soreness/strength loss vs rest
human: Recovery RCTs only; no longevity evidence
safety: Generally safe; combines heat and cold cautions
dose: ~1 min cold / 1-2 min hot, ~10-15 min total
caveats: Benefits limited to acute recovery; no evidence it affects aging biology
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Bieuzen et al., PLOS ONE 2013 — Reduced soreness/strength loss vs passive recovery [https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0062356]

name: Mesenchymal Stem Cell Therapy
mechanism: Infused MSCs act mainly via paracrine/immunomodulatory signaling to reduce inflammation and improve function
evidence: Longeveron's randomized Phase 2b (n=148, age 70+) for aging frailty did NOT meet its prespecified primary 6-minute-walk endpoint overall, but showed a significant dose-response — higher-dose arms improved 6MWT vs placebo with supportive patient-reported outcomes (Cell Stem Cell 2026). Among the better-controlled aging cell-therapy trials, but on functional surrogates; the wider 'stem cell clinic' market is largely unproven and risky.
effect: Dose-dependent 6-min-walk improvement (higher-dose arms); primary endpoint not met overall
human: One randomized Phase 2b positive on function; no hard-outcome/longevity data
safety: Generally well tolerated; infusion reactions; unregulated clinics pose real risks
dose: Single IV infusion of allogeneic MSCs
caveats: Primary endpoint missed; benefit limited to higher-dose subgroups on functional surrogates; commercial market largely unproven/risky
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Stem cell exhaustion; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Longeveron Phase 2b (Lomecel-B), Cell Stem Cell 2026 — Primary 6MWT endpoint not met overall; significant dose-response, higher-dose arms improved 6MWT vs placebo [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.stem.2026.01.017]

name: Quercetin
mechanism: Weak standalone senolytic (potentiated by dasatinib); anti-inflammatory, mild BP/glucose effects
evidence: As a standalone senolytic, quercetin is weak and cell-type-selective; most human senolytic data come from D+Q, not quercetin alone. Standalone RCTs show modest BP/glucose effects; bioavailability is poor.
effect: Modest, cell-type-selective senolysis; small BP/glucose effects
human: Limited standalone; mostly studied within D+Q
safety: Very safe at supplement doses; CYP3A4/P-gp interactions
caveats: Poor bioavailability and weak standalone senolytic activity; 'food senolytic' marketing overstated
hallmarks: Cellular senescence; Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Zhu et al., Aging Cell 2015 — Senolytic for senescent endothelial cells but not preadipocytes; D+Q broader [https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/acel.12344] | Quercetin BP meta-analysis — SBP -3 mmHg at >=500 mg/day [https://doi.org/10.1161/JAHA.115.002713]

name: UBX1325 (foselutoclax)
mechanism: Inhibits BCL-xL to kill senescent cells in diseased retinal vasculature
evidence: The most advanced senolytic in human trials — but in eye disease, on a surrogate (visual acuity), via local injection. In Phase 2b ASPIRE a single injection MISSED the primary non-inferiority endpoint vs aflibercept at weeks 20/24, reaching non-inferiority (not superiority) only by week 36. Says little about systemic aging.
effect: ~+5 letters visual-acuity gain; missed primary endpoint (reached non-inferiority, not superiority, to aflibercept by wk36)
human: Controlled Phase 2/2b ophthalmology data (local, not systemic)
safety: Well tolerated intravitreally
caveats: Strongest human senolytic data but confined to retinal disease and surrogate endpoints
hallmarks: Cellular senescence; Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: ASPIRE Phase 2b 2025 (n=52) — +5.2 letters at 24wk; missed the primary non-inferiority endpoint at wk20/24, reached non-inferiority by wk36; no intraocular inflammation [https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06011798]

name: Calcium Alpha-Ketoglutarate
mechanism: Co-substrate for dioxygenases (TET/JmjC); modulates epigenetic methylation, mTOR and inflammation
evidence: Best evidence is animal: in aged mice Ca-AKG extended lifespan ~12% and cut frailty ~46%. Human evidence is weak — the cited 'biological age -8 years' came from a small uncontrolled retrospective pilot; the controlled RCT (ABLE) is unpublished.
effect: Mouse healthspan/frailty large, lifespan ~12%; human 'age reversal' uncontrolled
human: Only a small uncontrolled retrospective pilot
safety: Well tolerated; AKG is endogenous
caveats: Marketed '8 years younger' rests on an uncontrolled n=42 pilot; controlled proof pending
hallmarks: Epigenetic alterations; Chronic inflammation; Deregulated nutrient sensing
keyStudies: Asadi Shahmirzadi et al., Cell Metab 2020 — Reduced frailty ~46% and extended lifespan (significant in females: median +16.6%; NS in males) [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32877690/]

name: Thymosin Alpha-1
mechanism: Modulates T-cell maturation and dendritic/TLR signaling, restoring lymphocyte function
evidence: Approved in several countries for hepatitis B/C with a good safety record, but its 'immune rejuvenation' longevity claim is weakly supported: the large Phase-3 TESTS sepsis trial found no overall mortality reduction. No RCT shows it slows aging in healthy adults.
effect: Restores T-cell function in immunocompromised states; no proven mortality/anti-aging benefit
human: Approved abroad for hepatitis; sepsis/COVID data largely neutral
safety: Very well tolerated; injection-site reactions; not FDA-approved in US
caveats: Real immunomodulatory effect, but 'anti-aging' use rests on weak/negative controlled evidence
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Wu et al., TESTS, BMJ 2025 (n=1,106) — 28-day all-cause mortality 23.4% vs 24.1% (HR 0.99); no overall sepsis-mortality reduction [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39814420/]

name: PQQ (Pyrroloquinoline Quinone)
mechanism: Stimulates mitochondrial biogenesis (PGC-1a/CREB) and acts as a redox antioxidant
evidence: One of few compounds shown to stimulate mitochondrial biogenesis in mammals. Small human RCTs report improved fatigue/sleep and raised BDNF/cognition in MCI, but all are small, short and surrogate.
effect: Modest fatigue/sleep and BDNF/cognitive-biomarker improvements
human: Only small short-term RCTs
safety: Well tolerated; long-term data limited
caveats: Tiny, short trials; clinical longevity relevance unproven
hallmarks: Mitochondrial dysfunction; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Nakano et al. fatigue RCT — 20 mg/d x8wk improved fatigue/sleep [https://doi.org/10.31989/ffhd.v2i8.81] | MCI RCT 2024 — Raised serum BDNF, improved some cognitive markers [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38908296/]

name: Resveratrol
mechanism: Proposed indirect AMPK/SIRT1 activation; direct sirtuin activation now largely discredited
evidence: The flagship 'sirtuin activator' story collapsed (the SIRT1 assays were artifacts). It failed to extend lifespan in healthy mice (ITP) and has poor bioavailability; human RCTs are mixed/mostly null. A poster child of hype outrunning evidence.
effect: None demonstrated in healthy mammals
human: Many RCTs, mostly null; no convincing lifespan/hard-outcome data
safety: Generally safe to ~1 g/day; GI upset; CYP inhibition (bleeding risk)
caveats: Poor bioavailability and debunked sirtuin mechanism; failed translation
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Mitochondrial dysfunction; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Strong et al., ITP 2013 — No lifespan extension in healthy mice [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22451473/]

name: EGCG (Green Tea Catechins)
mechanism: Antioxidant/metabolic signaling (Nrf2, NF-kB, AMPK); iron chelation
evidence: As concentrated extract, EGCG modestly improves some inflammatory/lipid markers, but the dominant clinical signal is dose-dependent HEPATOTOXICITY above ~800 mg/day. Whole-beverage green tea has far better safety and cohort data (separate entry).
effect: Small lipid/oxidative improvements
human: RCTs on biomarkers; safety, not efficacy, is the defining issue
safety: Dose-dependent hepatotoxicity above ~800 mg/d; take with food, avoid fasted
caveats: Hepatotoxicity at high doses; pro-oxidant at high concentrations
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Genomic instability; Cellular senescence
keyStudies: EFSA/COT statement — No hepatotoxicity below 800 mg/d EGCG; above that raises liver-injury markers [https://doi.org/10.2903/j.efsa.2018.5239]

name: Rhodiola Rosea
mechanism: Monoaminergic modulation; anti-fatigue, antioxidant and redox-balancing effects
evidence: Moderate, outcome-specific evidence for fatigue, stress and mild endurance/cognitive benefits; reviews note positive but methodologically limited trials (small, heterogeneous, some industry-funded). Symptom/performance surrogates only.
effect: Modest reductions in fatigue/stress; small ergogenic effects
human: Several small RCTs; quality limited; no longevity data
safety: Generally well tolerated; occasional jitteriness/insomnia
caveats: Trials small/heterogeneous; standardization varies widely
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Mitochondrial dysfunction; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Fatigue systematic review — Positive but methodologically weak/heterogeneous trials [https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/1472-6882-12-70]

name: Fisetin
mechanism: Senolytic flavonoid that clears senescent cells; antioxidant/Nrf2 effects
evidence: Strong preclinical credentials but a critical NEGATIVE ITP result: oral fisetin did not extend mouse lifespan in the rigorous NIA program. Human senolytic trials (AFFIRM) are ongoing/unpublished, so there is no positive human efficacy yet — popular hype outruns evidence.
effect: Mixed in mice; NULL in the gold-standard ITP
human: No published positive human RCT (AFFIRM unpublished)
safety: Generally safe, OTC; intermittent high doses in trials; long-term unknown
dose: Trials ~20 mg/kg x2 days, intermittent; OTC 100-500 mg/day
caveats: The most rigorous animal test (ITP) was NEGATIVE; human efficacy unproven; poor bioavailability
hallmarks: Cellular senescence; Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Yousefzadeh et al., EBioMedicine 2018 — Most potent senolytic flavonoid; extended lifespan in progeroid/aged mice [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2352396418303736] | NIA ITP 2023 — Fisetin did NOT extend lifespan in genetically heterogeneous mice [https://doi.org/10.1007/s11357-023-01011-0]

name: Gynostemma (Jiaogulan)
mechanism: AMPK activation (gypenosides); improves mitochondrial respiration and lipid/glucose metabolism
evidence: A plausible AMPK-activating botanical: a small crossover RCT showed increased muscle AMPK phosphorylation and improved mitochondrial function, and an Actiponin RCT showed anti-obesity effects. Trials small/short; no lifespan data.
effect: Modest metabolic/performance and body-fat effects
human: A few small RCTs on metabolic surrogates; no longevity data
safety: Generally well tolerated short term; mild GI
caveats: Small short trials (key AMPK RCT n=16, healthy untrained males only); variable gypenoside standardization
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Mitochondrial dysfunction; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: AMPK RCT 2023 (n=16) — Raised post-exercise muscle AMPK and O2 flux; lowered glucose/leptin [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10675532/]

name: Gotu Kola (Centella Asiatica)
mechanism: Stimulates collagen synthesis/wound healing; antioxidant; possible neurotrophic effects
evidence: Strongest human data are for wound healing and venous insufficiency; for cognition the human evidence is weak (a meta-analysis failed to show benefit), with most neuroprotective signals from aged-mouse studies. No human longevity data.
effect: Meaningful wound-healing/venous benefit; cognition unproven in humans
human: RCTs support wound/venous outcomes; cognitive/longevity benefit not established
safety: Generally well tolerated; rare hepatotoxicity/dermatitis
caveats: Cognitive/anti-aging claims rest largely on animal data
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation; Stem cell exhaustion
keyStudies: Wound-healing review 2024 — Accelerates wound closure (diabetic ulcers/burns) [https://doi.org/10.3390/pharmaceutics16101252] | Cognition meta-analysis, Sci Rep 2017 — No clear cognitive benefit in humans [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-017-09823-9]

name: Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy
mechanism: Intermittent 100% O2 at pressure creates a hyperoxic-hypoxic paradox triggering HIF, angiogenesis and claimed senolysis/telomere effects
evidence: The Hachmo 2020 trial reported 60 HBOT sessions increased immune-cell telomere length >20% and reduced senescent T-cells, with related Tel Aviv trials reporting cognitive/biological-age changes. These are small (n=35), single-center, uncontrolled surrogate studies; HBOT is approved only for specific indications.
effect: Telomere length +20-38% and senescent-cell reduction (surrogate, single-arm)
human: Small trials show biomarker changes; no RCT, no hard outcomes
safety: Barotrauma, oxygen-toxicity seizures, reversible myopia; clinic-supervised
status: FDA-approved for specific indications; anti-aging off-label
caveats: Telomere/senescence findings from one small uncontrolled study; needs RCT replication
hallmarks: Telomere attrition; Cellular senescence; Stem cell exhaustion
keyStudies: Hachmo et al., Aging 2020 (n=35) — B-cell telomeres +37.6%, senescent T-helpers -37.3% [https://www.aging-us.com/article/202188/text]

name: Cordyceps
mechanism: Proposed improved oxygen utilization and mitochondrial ATP; cordycepin may activate AMPK
evidence: Small RCTs suggest modest aerobic/exercise benefits (raised VO2max, time-to-exhaustion), often with multi-ingredient blends and short follow-up. Performance surrogates only; no longevity data.
effect: Modest VO2max/endurance improvements with chronic dosing
human: A few small (often multi-ingredient) RCTs; no longevity data
safety: Generally well tolerated; contamination risk in wild product
caveats: Most positive trials used multi-ingredient blends; species/quality vary
hallmarks: Mitochondrial dysfunction; Deregulated nutrient sensing; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Ergogenic review 2024 (5 trials) — Mushroom-blend VO2max +4.8 mL/kg/min after 3 weeks [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12986667/]

name: Reishi (Ganoderma Lucidum)
mechanism: Immunomodulation via beta-glucans (dectin-1/TLR-2); triterpene anti-inflammatory effects
evidence: A Cochrane review concluded reishi should not be first-line cancer treatment but may have an adjunct immune role; a healthy-volunteer RCT showed increased T-cell subsets and NK activity. Limited, immune-surrogate data, often low-quality; no survival/longevity data.
effect: Measurable immune-marker shifts; clinical benefit unproven
human: Limited RCTs on immune surrogates; no longevity data
safety: Generally well tolerated; antiplatelet interaction; rare hepatotoxicity
caveats: Product quality highly inconsistent; evidence base small/low-quality
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication; Cellular senescence
keyStudies: Jin et al., Cochrane 2016 — Insufficient for first-line cancer use; possible immune adjunct [https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD007731.pub3/full]

name: GHK-Cu
mechanism: Plasma tripeptide (age-declining) that modulates wound-healing, antioxidant and tissue-remodeling genes
evidence: A naturally occurring human-plasma tripeptide that stimulates collagen and skin repair. Credible human evidence is dermatologic/topical (improved post-laser healing, skin appearance); no human data support injectable/systemic GHK-Cu for lifespan, and copper dosing carries toxicity concerns.
effect: Real topical skin/wound-healing benefits; no systemic longevity evidence
human: Human evidence limited to topical/dermatologic use
safety: Topical generally tolerated; systemic/injectable risks copper accumulation; gray-market purity unverified
caveats: Genuine topical benefits do not translate to systemic anti-aging evidence; injectable use experimental
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation; Stem cell exhaustion
keyStudies: Pickart & Margolina, IJMS 2018 — Shifts gene expression toward tissue repair/antioxidant programs [https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms19071987]

name: Astragalus / Cycloastragenol / TA-65
mechanism: Claimed transient telomerase (TERT) activation to slow telomere attrition
evidence: The canonical 'plausible mechanism vs commercial hype' case: small sponsor-linked RCTs report telomere lengthening and fewer senescent T cells, but telomere length is a contested surrogate, products are costly, and telomerase reactivation carries a theoretical oncogenic concern.
effect: Measurable telomere lengthening of uncertain clinical meaning
human: Small (often sponsor-linked) RCTs on surrogates; no hard outcomes
safety: No serious AEs in <=12-mo trials, but long-term cancer risk theoretically plausible
caveats: Surrogate-only endpoints, small sponsor trials, high cost, theoretical oncogenic risk
hallmarks: Telomere attrition; Cellular senescence; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Salvador et al., Rejuv Res 2016 (n=117) — TA-65 increased telomere length vs placebo loss [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26950204/]

name: Low-dose Lithium
mechanism: Inhibits GSK-3b, enhances autophagy and neurotrophic signaling; trace lithium may be a micronutrient
evidence: A patchwork: trace lithium in drinking water inversely correlates with mortality in a large Japanese cohort, it extends lifespan in worms/flies, and a major 2025 Nature study showed brain lithium depletion in Alzheimer's with lithium orotate reversing pathology in mice. Human longevity data are ecological only.
effect: Worm/fly lifespan extension; human ecological mortality association
human: Ecological/observational only; no longevity RCT
safety: Therapeutic doses risk thyroid/kidney toxicity (narrow window); microdose/orotate appear safer but unproven
caveats: Human longevity evidence ecological/confounded; 2025 Alzheimer's findings preclinical
hallmarks: Disabled macroautophagy; Loss of proteostasis; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Zarse et al., Eur J Nutr 2011 — Higher tap-water lithium associated with lower mortality; extends worm lifespan [https://doi.org/10.1007/s00394-011-0171-x] | Aron et al., Nature 2025 — Lithium depleted in Alzheimer's brains; lithium orotate reversed pathology in mice [https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09335-x]

name: Thymus Regeneration (TRIIM)
mechanism: Growth hormone (with metformin/DHEA) regrows thymic tissue to restore naive T-cell output
evidence: The TRIIM pilot (n=9 men) reported thymic regeneration on MRI and ~1.5-2.5 year epigenetic age reversal — but it was very small, uncontrolled and used a confounded multi-drug regimen with GH's known risks. The expanded TRIIM-X trial is ongoing.
effect: ~1.5-2.5y epigenetic age reduction (tiny, uncontrolled pilot)
human: One small uncontrolled pilot; TRIIM-X ongoing
safety: GH risks: insulin resistance, oedema, carpal tunnel, theoretical cancer risk
caveats: n=9, no control, multi-drug confound; needs controlled replication
hallmarks: Stem cell exhaustion; Epigenetic alterations; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Fahy et al., Aging Cell 2019 (TRIIM) — n=9: thymic regrowth, ~2.5y epigenetic age reversal (uncontrolled) [https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/acel.13028]

name: Growth Hormone (HGH)
mechanism: Activates GH receptor and raises IGF-1; anabolic but drives pro-growth, pro-aging nutrient-sensing signaling
evidence: A cautionary tale: GH raises lean mass (Rudman 1990) but later RCTs found high rates of oedema, arthralgia, carpal tunnel and insulin resistance with NO functional benefit. The longevity literature points the OTHER way — low IGF-1 predicts human longevity, and GH excess (acromegaly) shortens lifespan. Supraphysiologic GH for anti-aging is biologically backwards.
effect: Surrogate body-composition change with harms; mechanistically pro-aging
human: RCTs show surrogate change with harms; observational data favor LOW GH/IGF-1
safety: Oedema, arthralgia, carpal tunnel, insulin resistance/diabetes; cancer concern; illegal for anti-aging in US
dose: Not endorsed; approved only for GH deficiency
status: FDA-approved (GH deficiency); anti-aging use illegal in US
caveats: One of the clearest cautionary tales: surrogate gains, real harms, mechanism opposing longevity
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Stem cell exhaustion; Genomic instability
keyStudies: Rudman et al., NEJM 1990 — +8.8% lean mass but later shown lacking functional benefit, with harms [https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199007053230101] | Milman et al., Aging Cell 2014 — Low IGF-1 predicts longer survival [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24618355/]

name: 17a-Estradiol
mechanism: Non-feminizing estrogen improving insulin sensitivity and reducing hypothalamic inflammation; effect depends on testicular hormones
evidence: A reproducible male-specific ITP geroprotector that extends male (not female) mouse lifespan even when started in mid-late life, via improved metabolic health. No human trials at all.
effect: +19% male median lifespan (mice; ITP site range ~9-26%)
human: No human longevity data
safety: Largely non-feminizing but reduces male fertility signaling in mice; human systemic safety unknown
caveats: Male-only, mechanism tied to male hormones; no human data; not the same as conventional 17b-estradiol
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Strong et al., Aging Cell 2016 (ITP) — +19% male median lifespan (across-site range ~9-26%); no female effect [https://doi.org/10.1111/acel.12496] | Garratt et al., Aging Cell 2018 — Benefit abolished by castration — depends on male hormones [https://doi.org/10.1111/acel.12786]

name: Pterostilbene
mechanism: Better-absorbed resveratrol analog; proposed AMPK/SIRT and antioxidant signaling
evidence: Pharmacokinetically superior to resveratrol, but human RCT data are thin and the key clinical finding is a SAFETY concern: monotherapy raised LDL cholesterol (~17 mg/dL), prompting a major supplier to halt orders.
effect: Modest BP reduction; clinically meaningful LDL increase
human: Few RCTs; main robust finding is an adverse LDL signal
safety: Raises LDL cholesterol; long-term CV implications unclear
caveats: LDL-raising effect is the standout caveat; longevity benefit unproven
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Chronic inflammation; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: Riche et al., 2014 RCT — Lowered BP but raised LDL ~17 mg/dL [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25057276/]

name: Partial Cellular Reprogramming
mechanism: Transient expression of reprogramming factors (OSK) resets the epigenetic age of cells without erasing identity
evidence: The most exciting frontier idea: in mice, partial reprogramming restored vision after optic-nerve injury and AAV-delivered OSK extended remaining lifespan ~109% in very old mice. Human work just began — Life Biosciences' ER-100 (eye) dosed its first patient in June 2026 — so systemic-aging benefit is unproven and cancer risk is the central concern.
effect: Mouse: large lifespan/function effects; no human efficacy data
human: First human dosing (eye, Phase 1) 2026; no lifespan/healthspan evidence
safety: Major theoretical risk of teratoma/cancer; only entering human safety testing
status: Preclinical for systemic aging; first localized human trial 2026
caveats: Spectacular mouse results but human evidence is first-in-human and eye-localized; systemic safety unresolved
hallmarks: Epigenetic alterations; Genomic instability; Stem cell exhaustion
keyStudies: Lu/Sinclair et al., Nature 2020 — OSK restored vision and reversed epigenetic age in mice [https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-2975-4] | Rejuvenate Bio, Cell Reprogram 2024 — AAV-OSK extended remaining lifespan ~109% in old mice [https://doi.org/10.1089/cell.2023.0072]

name: Oxytocin
mechanism: Hypothalamic hormone that (beyond social roles) supports muscle stem-cell activation and tissue regeneration; declines with age
evidence: An established human hormone with a regenerative role: in mice it is required for muscle maintenance and an oxytocin + TGF-b-inhibitor combination extended lifespan in old frail males. Human longevity data are minimal (a small intranasal study raised lean mass); no lifespan RCT.
effect: Muscle-regenerative/anti-frailty effects in mice; small human lean-mass signal
human: Long clinical-use safety record; anti-aging evidence preliminary/small
safety: Intranasal/low-dose generally tolerated; high-dose IV can cause hyponatraemia
caveats: Intriguing regenerative biology, but anti-aging benefit rests on one small study plus mouse data
hallmarks: Stem cell exhaustion; Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Elabd et al., Nat Commun 2014 — Restored aged muscle stem-cell activation in mice [https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms5082]

name: Apigenin
mechanism: Inhibits CD38, the main NAD+-consuming enzyme, indirectly preserving NAD+
evidence: A credible natural CD38 inhibitor that raises NAD+ and improves metabolic markers in rodents, but essentially no human trial measures NAD+ change with oral apigenin; the cited 'biological age' drop came from a multi-ingredient protocol. Poor oral bioavailability.
effect: Raises NAD+/metabolic markers in rodents; isolated human effect unquantified
human: No standalone human NAD+/aging RCT
safety: Generally safe dietary flavone; CYP interactions unclear
caveats: Human NAD+ evidence for isolated apigenin essentially absent; popular on mechanistic grounds
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Mitochondrial dysfunction; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Escande et al., Diabetes 2013 — Potent natural CD38 inhibitor; raised NAD+ in obese mice [https://doi.org/10.2337/db12-1139]

name: Thymalin
mechanism: Proposed to restore thymic/T-cell function and immune homeostasis ('peptide bioregulation')
evidence: Best known from Khavinson's Russian gerontology program reporting a ~2-fold mortality reduction in the elderly — but this is single-institute, open-label, non-blinded and never independently replicated in the West, so the dramatic figures are provocative but unverified.
effect: Reported large mortality reductions in one program; not credible without replication
human: Single-institute open-label data only; no Western RCT; LOW quality
safety: Reported well tolerated; gray-market product purity unverified
dose: 10 mg IM daily for 5-10 days, repeated
caveats: Headline mortality reductions rest entirely on unreplicated, non-blinded single-center data
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation; Stem cell exhaustion
keyStudies: Khavinson & Morozov, Neuro Endocrinol Lett 2003 — Reported ~2x mortality reduction (open-label, single-center) [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14523363/]

name: Pregnenolone
mechanism: Upstream precursor to all steroid hormones; neurosteroid modulating NMDA/GABA-A receptors
evidence: The upstream precursor of DHEA and sex steroids; levels decline with age, fueling supplement marketing. A proof-of-concept RCT in schizophrenia (Marx 2009) found pregnenolone reduced negative symptoms with some cognitive correlation, but there is no evidence of cognitive or healthspan benefit in healthy older adults, where controlled trials are scarce.
effect: Memory effects in aged rodents; no demonstrated human cognitive/longevity benefit
human: Sparse, largely negative RCTs; no longevity data
safety: Limited safety data; unpredictable conversion to androgens/estrogens/cortisol
status: OTC supplement; not approved for any indication
caveats: Marketed on animal data/mechanism; human evidence thin and mostly null
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Marx et al., Neuropsychopharmacology 2009 — Reduced negative symptoms in schizophrenia with cognitive correlation (disease population, not healthy aging) [https://doi.org/10.1038/npp.2009.26]

name: Procyanidin C1 (PCC1)
mechanism: Suppresses SASP at low dose; senolytic at higher dose via ROS/mitochondrial stress
evidence: A 2021 Nature Metabolism study reported strong single-lab mouse data — fortnightly dosing in very old mice extended remaining median lifespan ~64%. Not yet ITP-validated or tested in humans, and bioavailability of this large polyphenol is uncertain.
effect: Large effect on remaining lifespan in one mouse study; no human data
human: None
safety: Grape-seed proanthocyanidins generally safe as foods; isolated PCC1 not characterized
caveats: Single-lab mouse result now under a 2026 Editorial Expression of Concern (image-reuse, raw data unavailable); not ITP-validated or human-tested; OTC extracts aren't purified PCC1
hallmarks: Cellular senescence; Altered intercellular communication; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: Xu et al., Nat Metabolism 2021 — Biweekly PCC1 in old mice extended remaining median lifespan ~64% [https://www.nature.com/articles/s42255-021-00491-8]

name: NADH Supplement
mechanism: Supplies reduced NADH to support mitochondrial ATP; oral stability/absorption limited
evidence: Older, small, low-quality RCTs in chronic fatigue and open-label Parkinson's work with weak, inconsistent results; largely outside the modern NAD+ mainstream and of doubtful oral bioavailability.
effect: Weak/inconsistent symptomatic signals; no aging data
human: A few small, mostly old, low-quality studies
safety: Well tolerated; mild headache/GI
caveats: Dated, low-quality evidence and questionable oral bioavailability
hallmarks: Mitochondrial dysfunction; Deregulated nutrient sensing
keyStudies: Forsyth et al., 1999 — Small CFS crossover suggested symptomatic benefit (preliminary) [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10071523/]

name: Klotho Gene/Protein Therapy
mechanism: Restoring the age-declining longevity protein klotho enhances synaptic plasticity and resilience
evidence: A genuine circulating longevity protein: overexpression extends mouse lifespan, and a 2023 study showed a single low-dose injection improved memory in aged rhesus macaques. Supported by human genetics (KL-VS carriers), but no completed human therapeutic trials; the low-dose-only response complicates translation.
effect: Mouse lifespan + primate cognition; human effect of administration untested
human: Biomarker/genetic associations; no completed interventional trials
safety: No human safety dataset; affects phosphate/FGF23 axis; non-linear dose-response
caveats: Strong animal/genetic case but unproven and untested as a human therapy; hormetic dosing adds uncertainty
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Stem cell exhaustion; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Castner et al., Nature Aging 2023 — Single low-dose klotho enhanced memory in aged macaques [https://www.nature.com/articles/s43587-023-00441-x] | Kurosu et al., Science 2005 — Klotho overexpression extends mouse lifespan [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16123266/]

name: Fecal Microbiota Transplant (Heterochronic)
mechanism: Transferring young/healthy gut microbiota aims to reverse age-related dysbiosis and reduce systemic inflammation
evidence: In mice, young-to-aged FMT reverses gut/eye/brain aging hallmarks and improves cognition. Human aging evidence is essentially absent (FMT is approved only for recurrent C. difficile); applying it for longevity is preclinical, with documented infection risks.
effect: Mouse: reversal of gut/brain aging markers; no human aging effect shown
human: FMT proven for C. difficile only; no controlled aging data
safety: Infection transmission risk (incl. fatal cases); requires rigorous donor screening
status: Approved only for recurrent C. difficile
caveats: Striking mouse rejuvenation but no human aging evidence; real infection risk
hallmarks: Dysbiosis; Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Parker et al., Microbiome 2022 — Young-to-aged FMT reversed gut/brain aging markers in mice [https://doi.org/10.1186/s40168-022-01243-w]

name: Rilmenidine
mechanism: Engages nischarin/I1-imidazoline receptor, mimicking caloric restriction and inducing autophagy
evidence: An emerging CR-mimetic that extends lifespan/healthspan in C. elegans (even started late) and produces CR-like transcriptional changes in mouse liver/kidney. No mammalian lifespan study and no human longevity data; it is a well-tolerated antihypertensive.
effect: Lifespan extension in C. elegans; CR-like mouse signatures
human: No human longevity data
safety: Well tolerated as antihypertensive; longevity-use safety unknown
caveats: Evidence is worm lifespan + mouse surrogates only; no mammalian lifespan data
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Disabled macroautophagy; Loss of proteostasis
keyStudies: Bennett et al., Aging Cell 2023 — Extended worm lifespan via nischarin/autophagy; CR-like mouse transcriptome [https://doi.org/10.1111/acel.13774]

name: Humanin
mechanism: Cytoprotective peptide modulating apoptosis, IGF-1/IGFBP signaling and metabolic stress responses
evidence: A longevity-associated biomarker: circulating levels generally decline with age but are higher in centenarians and their offspring. Causal data are preclinical (overexpression extends C. elegans lifespan); no human interventional trials and no evidence that giving humanin extends human healthspan.
effect: Higher endogenous levels associate with longevity; exogenous benefit unproven
human: Observational/biomarker data only; no interventional trials
safety: No human dosing/safety dataset
caveats: Compelling longevity-associated biomarker, but therapeutic value in humans unestablished
hallmarks: Mitochondrial dysfunction; Altered intercellular communication; Deregulated nutrient sensing
keyStudies: Yen et al., Aging 2020 — Centenarians have higher humanin; overexpression extends worm lifespan [https://www.aging-us.com/article/103534/text]

name: Navitoclax (ABT-263)
mechanism: BH3-mimetic that triggers apoptosis of senescent cells via BCL-2 family inhibition
evidence: A potent senolytic in mice (rejuvenates aged stem cells, aids wound healing), but development for aging is blocked by on-target toxicity — BCL-xL inhibition kills platelets, causing severe thrombocytopenia. Studied clinically only in oncology.
effect: Strong senolytic in mice; no anti-aging human data
human: Oncology only; toxicity precludes longevity use
safety: Dose-limiting thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, bone loss
caveats: On-target platelet toxicity makes systemic anti-aging use impractical
hallmarks: Cellular senescence; Chronic inflammation; Stem cell exhaustion
keyStudies: Chang et al., Nat Med 2016 — Selectively killed senescent cells, rejuvenated aged stem cells in mice [https://doi.org/10.1038/nm.4010]

name: Young Plasma Transfusion
mechanism: Infusing young-donor plasma aims to deliver pro-youthful circulating factors (parabiosis-inspired)
evidence: Heterochronic parabiosis rejuvenates tissues in mice, but human evidence is weak: the Ambrosia trial was uncontrolled and pay-to-participate, drawing an FDA warning. Many researchers think DILUTION (removing old factors) explains the effect better than adding young factors.
effect: Robust rejuvenation in mice; no demonstrated human healthspan effect
human: Minimal, largely uncontrolled; FDA-flagged
safety: Transfusion risks (allergic reactions, TRALI, infection, overload); FDA cautioned against commercial use
status: Not approved for aging; FDA warning
caveats: Human benefit unproven and possibly attributable to dilution; commercial offerings unregulated
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Stem cell exhaustion; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Conboy et al., Nature 2005 — Parabiosis rejuvenates aged stem-cell function in mice [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15716955/] | FDA 2019 — Warned against young-plasma anti-aging infusions [https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/statement-fda-commissioner-scott-gottlieb-md-and-director-fdas-center-biologics-evaluation-and-0]

name: Telomerase Gene Therapy (TERT)
mechanism: AAV delivery of telomerase (TERT) re-extends telomeres, delaying replicative senescence
evidence: The Blasco-lab study showed AAV9-Tert in adult/old mice extended median lifespan 24%/13% without increasing cancer. Robust mouse evidence, but no rigorous human trials — human use is limited to unregulated self-experiments. Cancer risk remains the key concern.
effect: Mouse: +13-24% median lifespan; no validated human effect
human: No controlled human trials; only anecdotal self-experiments
safety: Principal concern is cancer (telomerase reactivation); AAV immunogenicity
caveats: Strong mouse data but zero rigorous human evidence; oncogenic potential unresolved
hallmarks: Telomere attrition; Cellular senescence; Genomic instability
keyStudies: Bernardes de Jesus et al., EMBO Mol Med 2012 — +24% (1yr) / +13% (2yr) median mouse lifespan, no excess cancer [https://doi.org/10.1002/emmm.201200245]

name: Mitochondrial Transplantation
mechanism: Isolated healthy mitochondria are delivered into damaged tissue to restore bioenergetics
evidence: Strong preclinical data show transplanted mitochondria reduce infarct size in ischemia models; limited human use is single-arm autologous transplantation in pediatric cardiac patients. No controlled aging evidence; the aging application is hypothetical.
effect: Animal: reduced infarct size; human: small uncontrolled cardiac use
human: Small single-arm ischemia use; no aging trials
safety: Early-stage; immunogenicity, delivery and durability are open questions
status: Early-clinical for ischemia; aging use conceptual
caveats: Human evidence tiny and disease-specific; longevity application speculative
hallmarks: Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: McCully et al., review 2021 — Reduced myocardial necrosis; small pediatric cardiac use

name: Minocycline
mechanism: Attenuates cytoplasmic translation of aggregation-prone proteins, improving proteostasis; anti-inflammatory
evidence: A proteostasis-targeting geroprotector that extended C. elegans lifespan and uniquely worked even in OLD worms (where most compounds fail). No mammalian lifespan or human longevity trial, and chronic antibiotic use raises resistance/microbiome concerns.
effect: Lifespan extension in C. elegans (incl. late-life)
human: No human longevity data
safety: Dizziness, photosensitivity, pigmentation, rare drug-induced lupus; chronic use disrupts microbiome
caveats: Worm-only lifespan data; antibiotic resistance/microbiome harm limit chronic use
hallmarks: Loss of proteostasis; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Solis et al., eLife 2018 — Extended worm lifespan even started late; of 21 compounds, only minocycline worked in old worms [https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.40314]

name: Senolytic Vaccine
mechanism: Vaccination against a senescent-cell antigen (GPNMB) directs the immune system to clear senescent cells
evidence: A 2021 study showed an anti-GPNMB vaccine cleared senescent cells, reduced atherosclerotic plaque, and extended lifespan in progeroid mice. Entirely in mice; a human vaccine is in development with autoimmunity as a key theoretical risk.
effect: Mouse: reduced senescence/plaque, extended progeroid lifespan; no human data
human: No human trials yet
safety: Theoretical autoimmunity (GPNMB not senescence-exclusive); untested in humans
caveats: Entirely preclinical; antigen specificity/autoimmune risk must be resolved
hallmarks: Cellular senescence; Chronic inflammation; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Suda/Minamino, Nature Aging 2021 — Vaccine reduced senescence/plaque, extended progeroid mouse lifespan [https://www.nature.com/articles/s43587-021-00151-2]

name: NK / Immune Cell Rejuvenation
mechanism: Expanded/engineered NK cells are infused to eliminate senescent cells and restore immune surveillance
evidence: NK cells naturally clear senescent cells, supporting adoptive NK therapy as 'senotherapy'. Evidence for the aging application is mechanistic/early proof-of-concept; NK therapy is clinically advanced in oncology, but no controlled trials show anti-aging benefit.
effect: Preclinical senescent-cell clearance; no demonstrated human aging effect
human: Proven in oncology; aging use mechanistic/early only
safety: Oncology NK therapy generally tolerable; aging-specific safety untested
caveats: No controlled human aging evidence; benefit inferred from senescent-cell biology
hallmarks: Cellular senescence; Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Immunity & Ageing 2024 review — Frames adoptive NK therapy as senescent-cell-clearing senotherapy [https://immunityageing.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12979-024-00451-2]

name: NAD+ IV Therapy
mechanism: Infuses NAD+ directly, though it is largely degraded to precursors before cellular uptake
evidence: Despite aggressive clinic marketing, controlled efficacy evidence for IV NAD+ in aging is essentially absent — systematic reviews find no eligible outcome trials. Tolerable short-term but benefits are anecdotal; expensive and clinic-administered.
effect: Unproven; no controlled outcome data
human: Only small tolerability/PK studies
safety: Infusion reactions (flushing, nausea, chest discomfort) if fast; unregulated clinic quality
caveats: High-cost, heavily-hyped with no controlled efficacy evidence and questionable bioavailability
hallmarks: Deregulated nutrient sensing; Mitochondrial dysfunction; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Systematic review 2026 — No eligible outcome trials of IV/IM NAD+ for anti-aging [https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1568163726000498]

name: Exosome Therapy
mechanism: MSC-derived exosomes deliver regenerative miRNA/protein cargo to modulate inflammation and repair
evidence: Preclinical and early human data suggest possible benefit for skin/hair, but human evidence is limited to small heterogeneous cosmetic studies. No exosome product is FDA-approved, the FDA has warned against marketed products, and manufacturing/standardization is unsolved.
effect: Possible modest dermatologic benefit; systemic/aging effects unproven
human: Only small cosmetic studies; no rigorous systemic aging evidence
safety: Unregulated products risk contamination/infection; FDA-flagged
caveats: Manufacturing unstandardized, market largely unregulated; systemic anti-aging claims unsupported
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: Systematic review 2025 — Preliminary dermatologic benefit; small/heterogeneous studies [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12736761/] | FDA warnings 2024-25 — Exosome products deemed unapproved [https://www.fda.gov/vaccines-blood-biologics/consumers-biologics/consumer-alert-regenerative-medicine-products-including-stem-cells-and-exosomes]

name: MOTS-c
mechanism: Exercise/stress-induced peptide acting via AMPK; regulates metabolic stress-response genes
evidence: An endogenous mitochondrial peptide that rises with exercise and declines with age; in mice late-life intermittent dosing improves physical capacity and healthspan. Essentially no controlled human efficacy trials and no human lifespan data; all human relevance is extrapolated.
effect: Robust metabolic/healthspan 'exercise-mimetic' effects in mice; human effect unknown
human: No controlled human efficacy trials
safety: No human safety dataset; gray-market injectable purity unknown
caveats: Promising mouse biology does not equal proven human benefit; sold ahead of evidence
hallmarks: Mitochondrial dysfunction; Deregulated nutrient sensing; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Reynolds et al., Nat Commun 2021 — Late-life MOTS-c increased physical capacity/healthspan in mice [https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-20790-0]

name: Grounding / Earthing
mechanism: Hypothesized transfer of Earth's electrons via skin contact to reduce inflammation (mechanism unestablished)
evidence: A few low-quality studies report sleep/pain/inflammation improvements, but the field is dominated by tiny samples, poor blinding and commercial conflicts. Mainstream reviewers consider the evidence too weak to support health claims; no rigorous replication.
effect: Claimed sleep/pain/inflammation benefits; not reliably demonstrated
human: Small low-quality studies; effect likely placebo
safety: Low physical risk; main risk is overhyped claims/opportunity cost
dose: Skin contact with ground / grounding products
status: Marketed wellness product; not medically recognized
caveats: Weakest evidence base in this set; claims rest on poor-quality, conflicted studies
hallmarks: Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Cleveland Clinic review 2022 — Evidence sparse, low-quality, insufficient to recommend [https://health.clevelandclinic.org/earthing]

name: Follistatin Gene Therapy
mechanism: Delivering follistatin inhibits myostatin/activin signaling, increasing muscle and reducing fat
evidence: Follistatin overexpression robustly increases muscle mass in animals. Human evidence is very weak — Minicircle's plasmid trial reports small, unpublished, offshore, self-pay results; no controlled efficacy or longevity data.
effect: Mouse: large muscle gains; human: small company-reported changes
human: Only an unregulated, unpublished offshore study
safety: Reported mild LDL increase; off-target risks of chronic myostatin inhibition unknown; gene-therapy risks
caveats: Human data unpublished, uncontrolled and commercially conflicted; longevity benefit speculative
hallmarks: Stem cell exhaustion; Deregulated nutrient sensing; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Minicircle trial (company-reported) — ~2 lb fat-free mass gain, minor LDL rise (unpublished) [https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06411366]

name: Epitalon
mechanism: Claimed telomerase activation and normalized melatonin/circadian function
evidence: Cell-culture work reports telomerase activation and rodent studies report lifespan effects, but human evidence is limited to small open-label/case series and the unreplicated Russian mortality program. Telomerase activation also carries a theoretical cancer concern.
effect: In-vitro telomerase/telomere effects and rodent claims; human longevity unproven
human: Only small open-label case series; very LOW quality
safety: Reported well tolerated; long-term unknown; theoretical oncogenic concern; gray-market purity
caveats: Heavily marketed 'telomere' peptide whose human evidence is essentially anecdotal/Russian-only
hallmarks: Telomere attrition; Epigenetic alterations; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Khavinson et al., Bull Exp Biol Med 2003 — Activated telomerase, extended fibroblast replicative capacity in vitro [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12937682/]

name: FOXO4-DRI peptide
mechanism: Disrupts FOXO4-p53 binding, triggering apoptosis selectively in senescent cells
evidence: Based largely on a single 2017 paper showing senescent-cell clearance and partial restoration of function in aged/progeroid mice. No human trials, limited independent in-vivo replication, yet heavily marketed in the gray-market peptide space.
effect: Mouse healthspan signals from limited studies; no human effect
human: None; no registered trials
safety: Unknown in humans; unregulated peptide purity concerns
caveats: Rests on one 2017 study; sold to consumers far ahead of human evidence
hallmarks: Cellular senescence; Genomic instability; Altered intercellular communication
keyStudies: Baar et al., Cell 2017 — Cleared senescent cells, restored fur/renal function in aged mice [https://www.cell.com/cell/fulltext/S0092-8674(17)30293-3]

name: BPC-157
mechanism: Proposed pro-angiogenic/cytoprotective effects (VEGFR2/NO) promoting tendon/gut/tissue healing
evidence: Extensive rodent literature suggests accelerated tendon/gut healing, but the human evidence base is essentially absent — no completed published RCTs. The FDA placed BPC-157 on its 503A Category 2 (significant-risk) list in 2023, then removed it in April 2026 pending an advisory-committee review (still NOT FDA-approved); its pro-angiogenic mechanism raises a theoretical tumor concern.
effect: Robust tissue-healing in rodents; no established human efficacy
human: No published human RCTs; widespread off-label/gray-market use
safety: No adequate human safety data; FDA-flagged over impurity/immunogenicity (Category 2 2023-26, since de-listed but still unapproved); theoretical cancer concern
status: Not approved; FDA 'do not compound' Category 2
caveats: Popular 'healing peptide' with NO human trial evidence and explicit FDA safety concerns
hallmarks: Altered intercellular communication; Chronic inflammation
keyStudies: Sikiric et al. (rodent studies) — Accelerated tendon/muscle/GI healing in rats | FDA 503A bulk-substances list — Category 2 (significant safety risk) 2023; removed April 2026 pending review, still not approved [https://www.fda.gov/drugs/human-drug-compounding/certain-bulk-drug-substances-use-compounding-may-present-significant-safety-risks]

name: Piperlongumine
mechanism: Degrades OXR1 selectively in senescent cells, raising ROS to trigger apoptosis
evidence: Senolytic activity is established essentially only in cell culture; no lifespan or controlled human studies. Most interest is mechanistic and as a scaffold for analogs.
effect: In-vitro senolysis; no in-vivo healthspan data
human: No human aging data
safety: Limited human safety data; reactive scaffold (its senolysis is ROS-independent, though piperlongumine is pro-oxidant in cancer settings)
caveats: In-vitro only; unproven safety, no lifespan data
hallmarks: Cellular senescence; Mitochondrial dysfunction
keyStudies: Wang et al., Aging (Albany NY) 2016 — Identified piperlongumine as a senolytic; killed senescent fibroblasts in vitro via ROS-independent apoptosis [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27913811/]
